project.title: Pipewright: End-to-End Data Pipeline for a CEO Dashboard
project.tagline: Build a production-style batch pipeline for an Indian D2C brand, from a messy API and late file drops to five trusted CEO reports: idempotent ingestion into a lake, dbt or PySpark silver and gold models that must agree row by row, data-quality checks behind a publish gate, CI, an Airflow schedule, a Streamlit dashboard in Docker, and a second release with incremental models, backfills, schema evolution and freshness alerts
project.description: BazaarBox, a direct-to-consumer home & kitchen brand, wants one dashboard that is correct by 06:30 IST every day: revenue by category and region, CAC by channel, Prime membership MRR, the top 10 products of the last 30 days and 30-day cohort retention. Over nine phases you build the pipeline behind it like a data engineering team: write requirements with SLAs and acceptance criteria, design the architecture, the bronze/silver/gold layers, a data contract and five ADRs (including why Airbyte, a Spark cluster and Metabase were swapped for lighter tools), then build it test-first. A seeded, offline copy of BazaarBox's systems (an orders and customers API with bearer tokens, cursor pagination, updated_at windows and injected 429/503 faults, plus daily payment, ad-spend and catalogue file drops) comes with real-world defects: mixed time zones, re-delivered orders, duplicate payment events, rupee amounts as text, city spellings, test orders and PII. You write idempotent ingestion into immutable lake partitions, silver and gold models in dbt (SQL track) or PySpark (Python track) whose gold tables must equal the golden files and each other row by row, declarative data-quality checks with severities and a publish gate built on an atomic swap, dbt data and unit tests, and a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs dbt build on a fixture and both tracks on the full history. v1.0.0 adds an Airflow 3 schedule, a Streamlit dashboard, an optional AI incident explainer with guardrails and an offline fallback, and a hardened Docker Compose stack under 6 GB of RAM. Then the pipeline meets its second month: a new channel and a new order status block publishing, coupons change the schema, and a partner file arrives late. You version the contract additively, make the facts incremental and prove them equal to a full refresh, add backfills, freshness, volume and SLA monitoring with alerts, prove backward compatibility with v1.0, and write a blameless post-mortem (v1.1.0). Everything runs on a laptop with no paid service and no API key.

outcomes: Turn a stakeholder request into exact metric definitions, SLAs and acceptance criteria that include bad and late data
Design a layered pipeline (bronze, silver, gold) with a data contract, a publish gate and ADRs, and justify tool choices against a RAM budget
Ingest a paginated, authenticated API and file drops idempotently, with retries, quarantine, manifests and PII dropped at the door
Parse time zones, business dates and money exactly, and build latest-version silver and gold reports in dbt or PySpark
Make two independent implementations agree row by row with golden files, and use that parity as a CI gate
Write dbt data tests, unit tests and enforced model contracts, and declarative data-quality checks with severities
Build CI in GitHub Actions: path filters, an aggregator check, dbt build on a fixture, Spark with Java, Airflow with constraints
Schedule the pipeline with Airflow 3, serve a tested Streamlit dashboard, and ship hardened Docker images under 6 GB
Add an optional AI incident explainer that only sees aggregate facts, is checked by guardrails and falls back to a template
Evolve a contract additively, build incremental models proven equal to a full refresh, run backfills, monitor freshness and SLAs, and write a post-mortem
Use AI assistants deliberately and verify every transformation they write
project.ai_feature: An optional AI incident explainer (`pipewright explain`, also on the dashboard's Data health tab): when a data-quality check blocks publishing, it receives only numbered aggregate facts from the check report (check ids, counts, thresholds and safe enum codes; never rows or customer data) and writes a short incident note for the on-call engineer. Guardrails reject any answer without a valid citation, with a number that is not in the facts, with a URL or with data-changing SQL, and the pipeline then uses a deterministic template, saying why. Offline by default; any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (a local Ollama, or a free tier) can be plugged in, and the key is never logged
project.portfolio_blurb: Built Pipewright, a production-style batch pipeline that turns BazaarBox's messy sources (a paginated orders/customers API with faults and late status changes, plus daily payment, ad-spend and catalogue file drops) into five CEO reports published by 06:30 IST: idempotent ingestion into immutable lake partitions with PII dropped at the door, silver and gold models implemented twice (dbt on DuckDB and PySpark) that agree row by row with golden files on four months of data, a data contract with severity-graded checks and dbt data and unit tests behind an atomic publish gate, GitHub Actions CI with cross-track parity, an Airflow 3 schedule, a Streamlit dashboard and a guard-railed AI incident explainer in a hardened Docker Compose stack under 6 GB. After a new channel and order status blocked publishing in the second month, v1.1 added an additive contract version with backward-compatibility checks, incremental facts proven equal to a full refresh, backfills, freshness/volume/SLA monitoring with alerts, a late-file drill and a blameless post-mortem.

phases.title: Setup, the brief and the sources
phases.heading: Phase 0 · Setup, the brief and the sources
phases.why_md:
A dashboard nobody can rebuild is a screenshot with a refresh button. Data teams start where engineers start: a
repository that installs with one command, source data whose origin you can prove, tests that say what "right"
means, and a log of how AI helped. In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, read the brief, meet
BazaarBox's sources (an API and three file drops) and their defects, run the starter, meet the pending tests and
the contract that will guide you, open your first pull request and start your `AI_LOG.md`. You will not write a
single transformation yet, on purpose: first you learn who needs which number, when, and what the sources can and
cannot tell you.
objectives: Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
Pick a track (SQL · dbt or Python · PySpark), install the toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux, and run `make lint test`.
Explain the brief in two sentences: who needs which five numbers, by when, and what a wrong number costs.

Generate the source data, prove it is exactly the published one (the manifest check), call the API stub with a token and list three defects you can see in the raw records, plus the two fields that must never reach the lake.
Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

steps.title: Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
steps.content_md:
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/end-to-end-data-pipeline` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**.
   The `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/end-to-end-data-pipeline.git
   cd end-to-end-data-pipeline
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/end-to-end-data-pipeline.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/end-to-end-data-pipeline`), not under `/mnt/c`.

steps.title: Install the tools for ONE track
steps.content_md:
Every track needs Git, `make` and Python 3.12: ingestion, the checks, the runner, the DAG and the dashboard are
shared Python. Run the doctor script; it tells you exactly what is missing:
```bash
scripts/doctor.sh
make setup            # .venv with the shared package and both tracks' pinned tools
```
`make setup` installs both tracks so you can run the parity check later; you will only *write* code in one.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt track:** dbt-core 1.12 with the DuckDB adapter. DuckDB is an in-process analytical database: no
server, the warehouse is one file, and it reads the lake's JSONL and CSV files directly. Your silver and gold
models are SQL files in `tracks/sql/models`; dbt builds them in dependency order, runs their tests and enforces
the column contracts.
```bash
.venv/bin/dbt --version                         # Core 1.12.x, duckdb 1.11.x
cd tracks/sql && ../../.venv/bin/dbt parse --profiles-dir .   # the project loads (no data needed)
```
Optional: the DuckDB CLI (`brew install duckdb`, or the binary from duckdb.org) to explore files by hand.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark track:** PySpark 4.2 in **local mode**: the Spark engine runs inside one JVM on your laptop, no
cluster. Your silver and gold models are DataFrame functions in `tracks/pyspark/pipewright_spark`; the gold
tables are written as Parquet and registered in the same DuckDB warehouse, so the checks and the dashboard do not
care which track built them. Spark needs Java 17 or 21:
```bash
java -version                                   # 17 or 21
.venv/bin/python -c "from pyspark.sql import SparkSession as S; s = S.builder.master('local[1]').getOrCreate(); print(s.version); s.stop()"
```
If Spark complains about the host name, set `export SPARK_LOCAL_IP=127.0.0.1`.
<!-- /track -->

steps.title: Read the brief
steps.content_md:
Read the top of `README.md` (the situation) and `contract/transform-spec.md` §1 (conventions). Write down, in your
own words: **who needs which number, how often, by what time, and what each kind of wrong number costs** (a revenue
figure that double-counts a duplicated payment? a CAC computed with test accounts? yesterday's dashboard shown as
today's?). Phase 1 turns your notes into requirements.

steps.title: Meet the sources
steps.content_md:
Generate the source data and check it is byte-for-byte the published one, then start the API stub:
```bash
make source            # generate → check against contract/source-manifest-1.0.json → serve on 127.0.0.1:18140
```
In a second terminal, look at the data the way an engineer does, from the outside:
```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18140/health
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:18140/v1/orders          # 401: a token is required
curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer bazaarbox-dev-token' \
  'http://127.0.0.1:18140/v1/orders?updated_since=2026-06-01T00:00:00%2B05:30&updated_before=2026-06-02T00:00:00%2B05:30&limit=3' \
  | python3 -m json.tool | head -60
head -3 source-data/drops/marketing_spend/spend_2026-06-01.csv
head -2 source-data/drops/payments/payments_2026-06-01.jsonl
cut -d, -f3 source-data/drops/products/products_2026-06-01.csv | sort | uniq -c
```
Read `source/README.md`. Then note three defects you can see without any code (two time-zone formats? amounts as
text with a rupee sign? the same payment event twice? a category with a leading space?), and find the two fields
the contract says must be dropped before anything is written (`contract/data-contract.yaml`, `pii_drop`).

steps.title: Run the checks and meet the pending tests and the contract
steps.content_md:
```bash
make lint test
```
All the tests are **skipped**. They are *pending*: the complete test suite is already written and switched off in
one `PENDING` list per suite:

| Suite | Pending list |
|---|---|
| shared package | `pipewright/tests/conftest.py` |
| SQL · dbt | `tracks/sql/pytests/conftest.py` |
| Python · PySpark | `tracks/pyspark/tests/conftest.py` |
| Airflow DAG | `orchestration/tests/conftest.py` |

Each entry names a milestone ("Phase 3 M2 - silver (staging) models"). In Phase 3 you delete one entry at a time,
watch the tests go red, and make them green.

Now open the files of `contract/` that make "right" precise (`contract/README.md` lists them all):
- `data-contract.yaml`: what each source must send, the enums, every gold table's columns and types, and the
  data-quality checks with their severities;
- `transform-spec.md`: every rule in words: parsing, silver, gold, the five reports;
- `fixture/source/` + `golden/fixture/`: three days of source data and the gold tables they must produce, small
  enough to check by hand; `golden/v1.0/`: the reference reports for the full three months.

steps.title: Your first pull request
steps.content_md:
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant explained a `java` / `dbt` / `pip` error during the
   install and how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab. Forks have Actions switched off until you click **"I understand my workflows, go ahead
   and enable them"**. CI runs lint + unit tests for the shared package and both tracks. Wait for green, fill in the
   PR template and merge.

ai_prompts.title: Fix my toolchain install
ai_prompts.prompt:
I'm on <Windows 11 + WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 | macOS 15 | Ubuntu 24.04>. I want to run a project that needs Python 3.12
with a virtual environment, <dbt-core 1.12 with dbt-duckdb | PySpark 4.2 in local mode with Java 21>, make and
shellcheck. Here is the output of scripts/doctor.sh: <paste output>. Give me the exact commands to install what is
missing, explain each one in one line, and tell me how to verify each install.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: running each verification command, re-running `scripts/doctor.sh` until every required line is green, and checking any download URL against the official site (python.org, adoptium.net, docs.getdbt.com, spark.apache.org, docs.docker.com). Never pipe an unknown URL into `bash`.

ai_prompts.title: Restate the brief as requirements
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is a stakeholder brief: <paste the "situation" paragraph of README.md>. Restate it as: (1) who needs which
number, at which grain, how often and by what time, (2) for each of the five reports, the questions I must ask
before I can define it exactly (which orders count as revenue? which day does an order belong to?), (3) three ways
the dashboard could show a plausible but wrong number, (4) what "fresh" and "correct" should mean, measurably.
Do not invent numbers or facts that are not in the brief.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking every claim against the brief (assistants add details that are not there, such as a revenue target or a data warehouse BazaarBox does not have), and keeping at least one failure mode about *time* (a time zone, a late update, a late file). `contract/transform-spec.md` §1 answers several of the questions.

ai_prompts.title: Read a source like a data engineer
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here are 3 records from a REST API of an e-commerce company and the header plus 5 rows of two daily CSV files:
<paste the curl output and the head of the spend and products files>. List every data-quality problem you can see
or suspect, how you would detect each one in code, which fields look like personal data, and what you would ask
the source owner. Do not write any transformation yet.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: finding each problem in the real data with `grep`, `cut | sort | uniq -c` or a quick DuckDB query (an assistant may "see" problems that are not in your sample), and comparing your list with `contract/transform-spec.md` §2-§3. These records are synthetic; with real customer data you would paste schemas and aggregates only, never rows with emails or phone numbers.

deliverables.text: Your fork contains the `solution` branch and the `phase-*` tags (`git tag -l` shows them).
`make lint test` passes locally (all tests skipped).
`make source` says the generated files are identical to the manifest, and you called the API with a token.
A note (in your PR description or `AI_LOG.md`): the five reports and their deadline, three source defects, and the two PII fields.
A merged PR with a green CI run.
`AI_LOG.md` has its first entry.

quiz.q: Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
options: Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
Otherwise the `solution` branch and the phase tags are missing from your fork
Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
Otherwise the source data is not copied
quiz.explanation: Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch; without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

quiz.q: Why does `make source` check the generated files against `contract/source-manifest-1.0.json`?
options: To prove your source data is byte-for-byte the data the golden tables were computed from, so a difference in your numbers is a bug in your code, not different input
Because Git cannot store JSONL files
quiz.explanation: The manifest lists the sha256 of every generated file. Same seed, same bytes. If the check fails, nothing downstream can be compared with the golden tables.

quiz.q: The orders API returns an order on 1 June and the same order again on 4 June. What happened?
options: The API has a bug and returns duplicates
The order changed (e.g. it was delivered or cancelled), so its `updated_at` moved into a later extraction window; the pipeline must keep the latest version
A customer placed the same order twice
quiz.explanation: Incremental extraction by `updated_at` sees every change of a record, so the same key appears in several daily partitions. Silver keeps the latest version per key (`transform-spec.md` §3.1). Counting both would double the revenue.

quiz.q: Why are all tests skipped in the starter?
options: CI is too slow to run them
They describe behaviour you build in Phases 3-6 and are switched on one milestone at a time
They only run on the solution branch
quiz.explanation: The full suite is written up-front (test-first). Deleting a line from a `PENDING` list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

quiz.q: Which fields must never reach the lake?
quiz.explanation: The contract's `pii_drop` lists them for the customers source. None of the five reports needs them, so the safest place to drop them is before the first byte is written: data you never store cannot leak.

quiz.q: Which of these may you paste into an AI prompt for this project?
options: Your `.env` file with an API key
500 customer records with emails and phone numbers
Column names, your own code, an error message and aggregate counts
quiz.explanation: Secrets and row-level personal data never go into prompts. The BazaarBox data is synthetic, but practise the habit you need at work: schemas, code and aggregates, not rows.

recap: A reproducible local environment for one track, checked by `scripts/doctor.sh` and `make lint test`.
The difference between `origin` (your fork) and `upstream` (the course repo), and why tags matter.
The brief as five numbers with a deadline, and the ways a dashboard can be plausible and wrong.
BazaarBox's sources from the outside: a paginated, authenticated API with incremental windows and three file drops, each with its defects.
The contract (data contract, transformation spec, fixture, golden tables, manifest) that defines "right".
The PR + CI loop and the habit of logging AI assistance without leaking secrets or rows.

phases.title: Requirements: the five reports, SLAs and acceptance criteria
phases.heading: Phase 1 · Requirements: the five reports, SLAs and acceptance criteria
phases.why_md:
"Revenue by region" sounds like a requirement. It is not one until you know which orders count (placed? paid?
delivered? not cancelled? not test orders?), which day an order belongs to (the customer's day in India, or the
server's day in UTC?), what happens when an order is cancelled a week later, and by what time the number must be
right. Most dashboard disputes are not bugs in SQL; they are two people with two definitions. In this phase you
turn the CEO's five questions into **written, testable definitions**, service levels for freshness and
correctness, and user stories with acceptance criteria that include bad and late data. Everything you build in
Phases 3-7 is checked against this document.
objectives: Name the stakeholders, the decision each one makes with the dashboard, and how often.
Define each of the five reports exactly: grain, measures, filters, the day an event belongs to, and an example row.
Write non-functional requirements with a measure and a test: freshness (by 06:30 IST), correctness (reconciliation), idempotency, privacy, footprint.
Write user stories with Given / When / Then acceptance criteria, including a late update, a duplicate event and a missing file.
Say what is out of scope for v1.0 and why.

steps.title: Stakeholders and their decisions
steps.content_md:
Copy `spec/requirements-template.md` to `spec/requirements.md`. Fill in §1: for the CEO, the Head of Marketing,
the Head of Category and Finance, write the decision they make with the dashboard ("move ad budget between
channels at the start of each month") and which report serves it. A report nobody decides with is a candidate
for "out of scope".

steps.title: Define the five reports precisely
steps.content_md:
For each report write: the question, the grain (one row per what?), every measure as a formula, the filters, the
date rule, and one example row you compute by hand from `contract/fixture/source`. Decide, and write down:
- Which order statuses count as revenue, and what happens to revenue when an order is cancelled or returned later?
- Which **calendar** decides the day: an order placed at 23:50 IST on 1 June is `2026-06-01T18:20:00Z`. Which day is it?
- Money: rupees with decimals, or integer paise? Why does it matter when you sum 18,000 order lines?
- CAC: spend divided by which customers? Test accounts? Customers whose channel is unknown? A month with no new customers?
- Prime MRR: how does an annual plan count? When does a cancelled subscription stop counting?
- Top 10: the last 30 days up to which date? Ties?
- Retention: "came back within 30 days" from which event? What about customers who signed up 10 days ago?

Compare your answers with `contract/transform-spec.md` §1 and §5 **after** you have written them. Where you
disagree, write down why: a good spec records the trade-off, not just the rule.

steps.title: Non-functional requirements (the SLAs)
steps.content_md:
Fill in §4 with a measure and a test for each:
- **Freshness:** yesterday's (IST) numbers are published by 06:30 IST; the dashboard always shows the business date
  it is showing.
- **Correctness:** every report reconciles to the order lines; a failed blocking check means the previous day stays
  published (a stale number is better than a wrong one).
- **Idempotency:** running the same day twice gives the same tables; re-running a past day replaces it.
- **Privacy:** no email or phone in the lake, the warehouse, the logs or any prompt.
- **Footprint:** runs on an 8 GB laptop and in free CI; no paid service.

steps.title: User stories with acceptance criteria
steps.content_md:
Write at least six stories in §3, each with Given / When / Then. At least three must be about **bad or late data**:
```text
Given an order placed on 2026-06-01 and cancelled on 2026-06-04
When the pipeline runs for 2026-06-04
Then the order no longer counts in the revenue of 2026-06-01, and the change is visible on the 2026-06-05 dashboard
```
Other good candidates: the payments file for a day is missing at 06:00; the same payment event arrives twice; a new
order status appears that the contract does not know; the API answers 429 for a minute.

steps.title: Sources, scope and open questions
steps.content_md:
Fill in §5 (what each source sends, when, and what can go wrong, from your Phase 0 notes), §6 (out of scope for
v1.0: e.g. real-time numbers, forecasting, per-customer views) and §7 (questions you would ask the CEO). Commit:
```bash
git switch -c docs/phase-1-requirements
git add spec/requirements.md AI_LOG.md
git commit -m "docs(spec): requirements for the five reports, SLAs and acceptance criteria"
```

quiz.q: An order is placed at 23:50 IST on 1 June. Its timestamp is `2026-06-01T18:20:00Z`. On which business day does it count?
options: 1 June: business dates are IST calendar days
2 June, because UTC is the standard
It depends on the server's time zone
Neither: orders near midnight are excluded
quiz.explanation: The contract fixes the calendar (`timezone: Asia/Kolkata`). Here the UTC date happens to be the same, but an order at 00:20 IST on 2 June is `2026-06-01T18:50:00Z`: grouping by the UTC date puts it on the wrong day. Never let the machine's time zone decide.

quiz.q: Why does the contract store money as integer paise?
options: Floating-point sums of thousands of rupee amounts drift by fractions of a paisa, so two correct pipelines can disagree; integers sum exactly
quiz.explanation: `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` in floating point. With integers, the SQL and PySpark tracks produce the same totals to the paisa, and the reconciliation checks can demand exact equality.

quiz.q: A blocking data-quality check fails at 06:05. What should the CEO see at 06:30?
options: The new numbers with a warning banner
Yesterday's last good numbers, clearly labelled with their business date, while the team investigates
Whatever the pipeline produced; checks are only advisory
quiz.explanation: A stale number that says it is stale is better than a wrong number that looks fresh. That is the publish gate you build in Phases 3-4.

quiz.q: Which acceptance criterion is testable?
options: "Given a payment event delivered twice, when the day is processed, then it is counted once in MRR"
quiz.explanation: A testable criterion names the input, the action and an observable result. The other three are wishes until someone defines accurate, gracefully and fast.

quiz.q: What belongs in "out of scope for v1.0"?
options: Things a stakeholder might expect but v1.0 deliberately does not do (e.g. intraday numbers), with the reason, so the expectation is managed early
quiz.explanation: Writing scope down prevents the worst kind of surprise: the one at the demo. It also gives v1.1 (Phase 7) a backlog.

quiz.q: Your assistant suggests "count revenue when the payment is captured" instead of by order status. What do you do?
options: Accept it: payments are more accurate
Treat it as a design question: check it against the brief and the sources (cash-on-delivery orders have no captured payment until delivery), and record the decision and its trade-off
Reject it: AI suggestions are never right
Implement both and let the CEO pick a number
quiz.explanation: It may be a good idea, but it changes the meaning of the number and depends on data you have not checked. A definition change is a stakeholder decision, written down, not an implementation detail.

recap: A metric is not defined until its grain, filters, calendar, money unit and late-data behaviour are.
Service levels for a data product: freshness, correctness, idempotency, privacy, footprint, each with a measure.
Acceptance criteria that include bad and late data, testable on a small fixture.
Scope as a tool for managing expectations, and open questions as part of the deliverable.

phases.title: Design: architecture, the data contract, layers and ADRs
phases.heading: Phase 2 · Design: architecture, the data contract, layers and ADRs
phases.why_md:
The old version of this project started with a tool list: Airbyte, Delta Lake, a Spark cluster, dbt, Airflow,
Metabase, Postgres. Together they need more than 16 GB of RAM, and none of them answers the questions that decide
whether the dashboard is right: where does each record land, can a day be re-run without duplicates, what happens
when a check fails, who may read a half-built table? Design is answering those questions **before** the code, and
choosing tools that fit the answers and the laptop. In this phase you draw the architecture, define the layers and
their contracts, read the data contract that pins every source and gold table, and record the five decisions that
shape the project as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).
objectives: Draw the pipeline: sources → ingestion → lake (bronze) → silver → gold → checks → publish → dashboard, and say what each step guarantees.
Explain bronze / silver / gold (the "medallion" layers): grain, mutability, who writes and who reads each.
Design idempotent ingestion: extraction windows, cursors, retries, partition replacement, manifests, PII handling.
Design a publish gate so the dashboard never reads a half-built or failed build.
Read `contract/data-contract.yaml` and say what each section enforces.
Justify every tool choice against the requirements and an 8 GB RAM budget, and write five ADRs.

steps.title: Draw the architecture
steps.content_md:
Copy `spec/design-template.md` to `spec/design.md` and draw §1 (Mermaid renders on GitHub):
```text
flowchart LR
  API[orders/customers API] --> ING[ingest]
  DROPS[file drops] --> ING
  ING --> BRONZE[(lake: raw, immutable)]
  BRONZE --> SILVER[silver: one clean row per entity]
  SILVER --> GOLD[gold: facts, dims, 5 reports]
  GOLD --> DQ{checks}
  DQ -- pass --> PUB[(published warehouse)]
  DQ -- fail --> INC[incident report]
  PUB --> DASH[dashboard]
```
For each box write one paragraph: input, output, the guarantee it gives the next box.

steps.title: Layers and their contracts
steps.content_md:
Fill in §2. Think about each row: **bronze** keeps every delivery exactly as received (minus PII), partitioned by
delivery date, never edited; silver and gold are always rebuilt from it, so a fixed rule fixes history. **Silver**
has one clean row per business entity (the latest order version, one row per payment event). **Gold** has the
facts, dimensions and the five reports, with the exact columns of the contract. Who may read silver? (Only gold
models.) Who may read gold? (Only through the published warehouse.)

steps.title: Ingestion that can be re-run
steps.content_md:
Fill in §3. Decide and justify:
- The extraction window for day D: `[D 00:00 IST, D+1 00:00 IST)` on `updated_at`, half-open, so no record is in two
  windows of the same run and none is missed at midnight.
- Pagination (follow `next_cursor`), retries (429/503 with exponential backoff and jitter, honour `Retry-After`;
  never retry a 401), a timeout on every request.
- Writing: the day's partition is written to a temporary directory and swapped in whole; re-running D replaces it.
  A manifest records what was loaded (counts, sha256, contract version).
- Bad records: rows missing a required field go to `lake/quarantine/` with the reason, not into bronze, and are counted.
- PII: `email` and `phone` are dropped before the first byte is written.

steps.title: Read the data contract
steps.content_md:
Open `contract/data-contract.yaml` and annotate (in your design) what each section enforces:

| Section | Enforced by | When it fails |
|---|---|---|
| `sources` (required fields, primary key, `pii_drop`) | ingestion | the record is quarantined; PII never lands |
| `enums` | `accepted_values` checks, dbt tests | the build is not published |
| `gold` (columns, types, order) | dbt model contracts / PySpark `enforce()` | the build fails before it is checked |
| `checks` (severity `error`/`warn`) | `pipewright dq` | `error`: not published; `warn`: published, reported |

Then read `contract/transform-spec.md` once end to end and mark the three rules you think are easiest to get wrong.

steps.title: The publish gate
steps.content_md:
Fill in §5. The dashboard reads `warehouse/pipewright.duckdb`. Every run builds into a **separate build file**,
runs the checks on it, records the verdict in the build itself (`ops.build_info`), and only then swaps the build
into place with one atomic rename. A crash, a failed check or a half-written table can therefore never reach the
dashboard: it keeps the last good build, which knows its own business date.

steps.title: Tools and footprint
steps.content_md:
Fill in §7. For each tool of the old design, decide keep / replace and why, with the RAM it needs on a laptop.
Then compare with the reference decisions (after writing yours): `git show phase-2-end:spec/design.md`.

through the `lake_glob()` macro, never the API; materialized as tables so the published file is self-contained), `models/gold` (tables, with `contract: {enforced: true}` so the
column names and types of `data-contract.yaml` are checked at build time), seeds (`city_map`), and where the tests

deliverables.text: `spec/design.md` with the architecture diagram and all eight sections.
A layer table (bronze / silver / gold) with grain, mutability, writers and readers.
An ingestion design that explains windows, retries, idempotent partition writes, quarantine and PII handling.
The publish gate described so that a crash at any point leaves the dashboard on the last good build.
Five ADRs in `spec/adr/`.
An `AI_LOG.md` entry, including one AI suggestion you rejected and why.

quiz.q: Why is the bronze layer immutable and partitioned by delivery date?
options: Because files are cheaper than tables
So silver and gold can always be rebuilt from exactly what was received; a fixed rule fixes history, and re-running a day replaces only that day's partition
quiz.explanation: If bronze were edited in place you could never reproduce yesterday's numbers or replay a bug fix over history. Partitioning by delivery date makes a re-run replace one partition, never append duplicates.

quiz.q: Why is the API extraction window half-open, `[D 00:00 IST, D+1 00:00 IST)`?
options: So every instant belongs to exactly one window: a record updated exactly at midnight is loaded once, not twice or never
quiz.explanation: Closed windows `[a, b]` double-load records at the boundary; open ones lose them. Half-open windows tile the time line exactly.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of building into a separate file and swapping it in with one rename?
options: The dashboard can only ever see a complete build that passed its checks; a crash or a failed check leaves the last good warehouse in place
DuckDB cannot write to an open file
quiz.explanation: `os.replace` on the same file system is atomic: readers see either the old file or the new one, never a half-written one. The checks run before the swap, so a failed build is never visible.

quiz.q: Why did the design replace Airbyte with a small ingestion package?
options: For one API and three files, a platform needing several GB of RAM and many containers hides the very ideas the project teaches (windows, cursors, retries, idempotency); a few hundred lines of tested Python show them and run on any laptop
quiz.explanation: At work, a connector platform is often the right call for dozens of sources. Here the ADR records the trade-off: fewer moving parts and full visibility, at the cost of writing (and testing) the connector yourself.

quiz.q: What does an `error` severity on a contract check mean?
options: The build is not published: the dashboard keeps the last good data and an incident report is written
quiz.explanation: `warn` checks are published and reported; `error` checks block the publish gate. Deleting rows to make a check pass would hide the problem.

quiz.q: Why must every model filter lake partitions with `dt <= run_date`?
options: So a build for a past day (a backfill or a re-run) sees only what had arrived by then and gives the same numbers as the original run
quiz.explanation: Without it, rebuilding 15 June after September's data has landed would mix in later status changes and give different numbers than the dashboard showed on 16 June. Reproducibility needs a time boundary.

recap: An architecture expressed as guarantees between steps, not as a tool list.
Medallion layers with clear grain, mutability and access rules.
Idempotent ingestion: half-open windows, retries with backoff, partition replacement, manifests, quarantine, PII at the door.
A publish gate built on an atomic rename.
Tool choices justified against requirements and a RAM budget, recorded as ADRs.

phases.title: Implementation in four milestones: ingest, silver, gold, run
phases.heading: Phase 3 · Implementation in four milestones: ingest, silver, gold, run
phases.why_md:
This is where most pipelines quietly go wrong: an order counted twice because it changed status, a payment event
delivered twice, a timestamp shifted by five and a half hours because the server runs in UTC, rupees summed as
floats, a re-run that appends a second copy of yesterday. You build the pipeline **test-first**, one milestone at a
time: delete a line from a `PENDING` list, watch its tests fail, implement until they pass. Every function and model
has a `TODO` with a hint that says where in `contract/transform-spec.md` to look and which trap to avoid. At the end,
one command ingests three months of BazaarBox data, builds silver and gold, and publishes a warehouse whose five
reports match the golden tables to the paisa.
objectives: Ingest an API with windows, pagination and retries, and file drops with validation, into idempotent lake partitions without PII (M1).
Parse mixed time-zone timestamps, IST business dates and rupee text exactly, and build silver: the latest version per key, one row per event (M2).
Build the gold dimensions, facts and the five reports with the exact contract columns (M3).
Run the whole thing for a date or a range, publish atomically, and schedule it with an Airflow DAG (M4).
Prove your gold tables equal `contract/golden/` on the fixture and on the full history.

steps.title: The red-green loop
steps.content_md:
For every milestone:
1. Delete the milestone's line from the `PENDING` list in **every** conftest that has it
   (`pipewright/tests/conftest.py`, `tracks/<your track>/.../conftest.py`, `orchestration/tests/conftest.py`).
2. Run the tests: they fail with `NotImplementedError: Phase 3 Mx ...` (red).
3. Implement one function or model at a time, re-running the tests (green). Commit after each green step:
   `feat(pipewright): M1 HTTP client with backoff and Retry-After`.
4. Never edit a test to make it pass. If you believe a test is wrong, open an issue quoting the spec section.
```bash
make test-pipewright          # the shared package
make test-sql                 # or: make test-pyspark
make lint                     # ruff, sqlfluff, shellcheck: keep it green as you go
```
Find every stub of a milestone with `grep -rn "Phase 3 M1" pipewright tracks orchestration`.

steps.title: M1: ingestion (shared by both tracks)
steps.content_md:
Remove `"Phase 3 M1 - ingestion"`. Implement, in this order:
1. `pipewright/http.py`: `HttpClient.delay` (exponential backoff with jitter, capped; honour a numeric
   `Retry-After`) and `get_json` (bearer token, timeout, retry 429/5xx/connection errors up to `max_attempts`,
   **never** retry 401 or other 4xx; raise `SourceError` when retries run out).
2. `pipewright/lake.py`: `write_partition`: write every file into a temporary sibling directory, then swap it in
   with a rename, so a crash leaves either the old partition or the new one.
3. `pipewright/ingest.py`: `fetch_window` (the half-open window from `config.window(day)`, follow `next_cursor`),
   `conform` (drop `pii_drop` fields, reject rows missing a required field), `ingest_api`, `validate_file`,
   `ingest_file` (a missing drop raises `MissingDrop` → exit code 3).

Try it against the stub (`make source` in another terminal):
```bash
.venv/bin/pipewright ingest --all --date 2026-06-01
ls lake/raw/*/dt=2026-06-01/ && cat lake/_manifests/orders/2026-06-01.json
grep -c email lake/raw/customers/dt=2026-06-01/* || echo "no PII in the lake"
.venv/bin/pipewright ingest --all --date 2026-06-01 && find lake/raw -type f | wc -l    # same count: idempotent
SOURCE_FAULT_RATE=0.3 make source      # restart the stub with faults; ingestion must still succeed
```
The track suites use M1 too: their fixtures ingest the 3-day fixture through your code (`pipewright.testkit`).

steps.title: M2: silver (staging) models
steps.content_md:
Remove `"Phase 3 M2 - silver (staging) models"`. Start with parsing (`transform-spec.md` §2), then one model per
source (§3.1-§3.6). The tests compare every silver table with `contract/golden/fixture-silver/`.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt:** implement the macros in `tracks/sql/macros/parsing.sql` (`utc_timestamp`, `ist_date`, `to_paise`),
then the models in `models/staging/`. Read the lake with `read_json(... '{{ lake_glob("orders", "jsonl") }}' ...)`
and `filename=true` to get the partition `dt`; keep only `dt <= {{ run_date() }}`. The latest version per key is a
window function:
```sql
qualify row_number() over (partition by order_id order by updated_at_utc desc, dt desc) = 1
```
Unnest order items together with their position (`unnest(generate_series(1, len(items)))` next to `unnest(items)`
in the same select) so `line_number` is the 1-based position in the *original* array, then drop `qty <= 0`. Run one model at a time:
```bash
cd tracks/sql && ../../.venv/bin/dbt build --profiles-dir . --select stg_orders --vars '{run_date: "2026-06-03"}'
```
(The tests run dbt for you against a temporary build of the fixture; this command is for exploring.)
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark:** implement `pipewright_spark/parsing.py` (`utc_timestamp`, `ist_date`, `to_paise`,
`clean_key` as **column expressions**: no Python UDFs, so Spark can optimise them), then `staging.py`. Bronze is read
by `bronze.py` with explicit schemas. The latest version per key is a window:
```python
w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.col("updated_at_utc").desc(), F.col("dt").desc())
df.withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w)).where("_rn = 1").drop("_rn")
```

quiz.q: An order appears in the lake on 1 June (placed) and on 4 June (cancelled). What does silver keep?
options: Both rows, so the history is visible
One row: the latest version by `updated_at` (then `dt`), with status `cancelled`
The first row, because it has the original amount
quiz.explanation: Bronze keeps both deliveries (immutable history); silver keeps the latest state per `order_id` (§3.1). Keeping both would double-count the order's lines in revenue.

quiz.q: Why must `HttpClient` never retry a 401?
options: A wrong or missing token will not fix itself; retrying wastes time and can lock the account, so it must fail fast with a clear error
Retries are only for GET requests
quiz.explanation: Retry what is transient (429, 5xx, timeouts), fail fast on what is not (401, 404, 400). Honour `Retry-After` when the server tells you how long to wait.

quiz.q: `2026-06-01T19:00:00Z`: which business date is it?
quiz.explanation: `ist_date(ts) = date(ts + 5h30)`. Grouping by the UTC date puts every order between 00:00 and 05:30 IST on the wrong day; the fixture contains such orders on purpose.

quiz.q: Why does `line_number` keep the position in the *original* items array even when a line with `qty <= 0` is dropped?
options: So the key `(order_id, line_number)` of every kept line is stable: dropping or fixing another line never renumbers it
quiz.explanation: Keys that shift when unrelated data changes break incremental updates, joins with downstream systems and parity between tracks.

quiz.q: Why is the warehouse published with `os.replace` instead of writing the tables directly into it?
options: The rename is atomic: the dashboard sees the complete old build or the complete new build, never a half-written one
quiz.explanation: Write to a build file, check it, then swap. A crash or a failed check before the swap leaves the published file untouched.

quiz.q: Your PySpark CAC uses `F.floor(spend / customers)` and one row differs from golden by 1 paisa. Why?
options: `/` produces a double; for large values a double cannot represent every integer quotient exactly, so flooring it can be off by one; integer division avoids it
quiz.explanation: Money stays integer end to end. Use integer division (`div`) so both tracks round down exactly as the spec says.

phases.title: Data tests and data-quality checks: the publish gate
phases.heading: Phase 4 · Data tests and data-quality checks: the publish gate
phases.why_md:
Unit tests prove your code does what you meant on the inputs you thought of. Data does not care what you thought
of: tomorrow the source sends a status nobody announced, a catalogue drop forgets a SKU, a join fans out after a
schema change. A pipeline needs a second kind of test that runs **on every build, on the real data, before anyone
sees it**: data tests and data-quality checks. In this phase you switch on the checks declared in the data contract,
write the dbt data tests and unit tests (SQL track), add a coverage gate, and see the publish gate do its job: a
build that fails a blocking check is never published, and an incident report explains why.
objectives: Explain the difference between unit tests (code, small inputs), data tests (properties of the real tables) and data-quality checks (the gate before publishing).
Implement the contract's check kinds: `row_count_min/max`, `accepted_values`, `relationship`, `max_share`, `expression`, `reconcile`, with severities.
Record only aggregates in the report (never a row), and mask unexpected values that might be personal data.
Write dbt generic, singular and unit tests (SQL track) or rely on the shared checks plus a coverage gate (PySpark track).
Break the data on purpose and watch the gate keep the last good build.

steps.title: Three kinds of tests
steps.content_md:
Write one sentence each in your notes, then read on:
- **Unit test:** a function or model on a tiny, hand-made input (`test_parsing.py`, a dbt unit test). Runs in CI.
- **Data test:** a property every row or table must have (`order_id` is unique, every order's customer exists, revenue
  reconciles to the lines). Runs on every build, on the real data.
- **Data-quality check with a severity:** a data test wired to a decision: `error` blocks publishing, `warn` is
  published and reported. Lives in `contract/data-contract.yaml` so both tracks share it.

steps.title: Implement the contract's checks (shared)
steps.content_md:
Remove `"Phase 4 - data-quality checks"` from every `PENDING` list. Implement `pipewright/dq.py`'s `run_check`: one
branch per kind. Each runs **one aggregate query** against the build and returns a `CheckResult` with `observed`,
`threshold` and `status`:
- `accepted_values`: count rows outside the list (`@order_status` resolves to the contract's enum); report up to 5
  distinct unexpected values, masked unless they match `SAFE_VALUE` (a code is fine, an email is not).
- `relationship`: count child keys with no parent. `max_share`: the share of rows matching `where`.
- `reconcile`: two queries that must return the same number (revenue = revenue lines).
- A check that cannot run (bad SQL, unknown kind) is status `error`, **never** a pass.

steps.title: A coverage gate
steps.content_md:
Add `fail_under = 85` to `[tool.coverage.report]` in `pipewright/pyproject.toml` (and `tracks/pyspark/pyproject.toml`
on the PySpark track). `make test-pipewright` now fails if less than 85 % of the lines ran. Look at the report's
missing lines: an untested branch in ingestion or in a check is exactly where a 3 a.m. surprise hides. Coverage is a
floor, not a goal: 100 % covered code can still compute the wrong revenue; that is what the golden tables are for.

steps.content_md:
Prove the gate works, end to end, on a copy of the data:
```bash
cp -r source-data /tmp/broken && sed -i 's/"status":"delivered"/"status":"lost"/' /tmp/broken/api/orders.jsonl
# restart the stub on /tmp/broken (python -m bazaarbox_source serve --data /tmp/broken --port 18140), then:
.venv/bin/pipewright run --date 2026-08-31; echo "exit $?"
ls warehouse/reports/ && .venv/bin/pipewright explain           # the incident note (template until Phase 6)
```

quiz.q: What is the difference between a unit test and a data test?
options: A unit test checks code on small hand-made inputs in CI; a data test checks a property of the real tables on every build
Data tests are slower unit tests
Unit tests are only for Python
quiz.explanation: Code can be correct and the data still wrong (a new status, a missing SKU). You need both: unit tests before merging, data tests before publishing.

quiz.q: A check fails because 41 orders have a status the contract does not know. What should happen?
options: Map the new status to `placed` and continue
Block the publish (severity error), keep the last good warehouse, write an incident report naming the unexpected value
quiz.explanation: An unknown status could be revenue or a loss; guessing silently changes the CEO's numbers. The contract decides, and changing it is a versioned decision (Phase 7).

quiz.q: Why must a check that cannot run (e.g. a SQL error) be reported as `error`, not `pass`?
options: A check that silently passes when it is broken gives false confidence: the gate would be open exactly when it is blind
quiz.explanation: Fail closed. A broken smoke detector must beep, not stay quiet.

quiz.q: Why does the report store "41 rows, values: lost" and never the 41 rows themselves?
options: The report is shared with on-call engineers and an AI model: aggregates and safe codes are enough to act on, rows could contain personal data
quiz.explanation: Design reports so they can be shared. Values that do not look like a code are masked for the same reason.

quiz.q: What does `reconcile` between `mart_revenue_daily` and `fct_order_items` catch?
options: A join or filter that drops or duplicates revenue between the facts and the report, even when every column looks valid
quiz.explanation: Column tests cannot see a fan-out: every row is valid, there are just too many. Totals that must agree across layers can.

quiz.q: Your coverage is 92 %. Does that mean the revenue is right?
options: No: coverage says which lines ran, not whether they compute the right number; the golden tables and reconciliation checks test correctness
Coverage does not apply to data pipelines
quiz.explanation: Coverage finds untested code; it cannot find a wrong rule that is tested with a wrong expectation.

phases.title: CI: dbt build and tests on the fixture, cross-track parity
phases.heading: Phase 5 · CI: dbt build and tests on the fixture, cross-track parity
phases.why_md:
A pipeline's code changes far more often than its sources: a "harmless" refactor of a join, a dbt upgrade, a new
column. Each can move a number the CEO reads tomorrow. Continuous integration runs every check on every pull
request, on a clean machine, before the change is merged: lint, the unit tests, **`dbt build` with all its tests on
the committed fixture**, the DAG tests, and the strongest check of all: both tracks run the full history and must
produce the golden tables and each other's tables, row by row. In this phase you replace the starter's simple CI
with that pipeline, learn every GitHub Actions concept it uses, and make one check, `ci-ok`, the gate for merging.
objectives: Read and write a GitHub Actions workflow: triggers, jobs, `needs`, `if`, matrix, caching, outputs, artifacts, permissions.
Run each part only when its files changed (path filters) without blocking pull requests (an aggregator job).
Check in CI that the committed fixture and manifest are exactly what the seeded generator produces.
Run `dbt build` (models, data tests, unit tests, contracts) on the fixture, and the PySpark suite with Java, in CI.
Run the full-history parity of both tracks in CI and publish its result on the run page.
Keep CI's tool versions identical to your laptop's, and protect `main` with required checks.

steps.title: Read the starter CI and the explainer
steps.content_md:
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the starter: one matrix job per part, `make install/lint/test-<part>`) next to
`docs/github-actions-explained.md` §1-§6. Answer for yourself: which event starts it, how many jobs run, where the
Python version comes from, why `fail-fast: false`.

steps.title: Design the full pipeline
steps.content_md:
Sketch the jobs and their dependencies before writing YAML:
```text
changes ─┬─ contract        (fixture + manifest reproducible, shellcheck, CMS export)
         ├─ pipewright      (lint + tests + coverage gate)
         ├─ sql ──────┐     (sqlfluff + dbt build on the fixture + expected tables)
         ├─ pyspark ──┼─ parity   (full history, both tracks = golden, sql = pyspark)
         ├─ orchestration   (DAG tests, Airflow constraints)
         └──────────────┴─ ci-ok   (fails if anything failed; skipped is fine)
```
Keep the job names `pipewright · lint + unit`, `sql · lint + unit`, `pyspark · lint + unit`: branch protection
already requires them.

steps.title: Write the workflow
steps.content_md:
Replace `.github/workflows/ci.yml` step by step (the reference is `git show phase-5-end:.github/workflows/ci.yml`;
write yours first):
1. `changes` with `dorny/paths-filter@v3` and an `all` output that is true on pushes or when shared files changed
   (`github-actions-explained.md` §7).
2. `contract`: regenerate the 3-day fixture into `$RUNNER_TEMP` and `diff -r` it with `contract/fixture/source`;
   regenerate the full source with `--check contract/source-manifest-*.json`; `shellcheck scripts/*.sh`;
   `python3 scripts/build-cms.py --check`.
3. One job per part with `actions/setup-python@v5` (Python 3.12, `cache: pip`), `actions/setup-java@v4` (Temurin 21)
   for PySpark, and the same `make` targets you run locally.
4. `orchestration`: install Airflow **with its constraints file** and run `make test-orchestration`.
5. `parity`: both tracks + Java, then `scripts/parity-run.sh <version>`; append the output to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`.
6. `ci-ok`: `if: always()`, `needs:` everything, fail on `failure` or `cancelled`.

Lint it before pushing: `actionlint` (<https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint>) catches typos in expressions and
runs shellcheck on every `run:` block.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt track:** the `sql` job is where dbt runs in CI: `make test-sql` builds the fixture with `dbt build` (seeds,
models, contracts, data tests, unit tests) through the same runner as production, then compares silver and gold with
the expected files. Add `--warn-error-options` only if you want warnings to fail too (we allow `warn` severity). The
`target/` folder is never committed: CI starts clean, so a model that only works because of a stale artifact fails here.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark track:** the `pyspark` job needs `actions/setup-java@v4` before the tests, or Spark fails with
"JAVA_HOME is not set". Spark is slow to start: one session per test run (the `spark` fixture), `local[2]`, and a
`timeout-minutes` on the job so a hung JVM cannot burn six hours of free minutes.
<!-- /track -->

steps.content_md:
1. Push a branch and open a PR: watch the jobs start, the skipped ones, and `ci-ok`.
2. Make it fail on purpose: change one rule (e.g. `>= 0` to `> 0` in a model), push, and read the `parity` summary.
   Revert.

ai_prompts.prompt:
Here is a GitHub Actions workflow: <paste ci.yml>. Explain it to a data engineer who has never used Actions: what
triggers it, which jobs run in which order and why, what each `if:` decides, what is cached and with which key.

ai_prompts.title: Debug a red CI job
ai_prompts.prompt:
This CI job fails but the same command passes on my laptop. Job log (last 60 lines): <paste>. Workflow job: <paste
the job>. My local versions: <python --version, java -version, pip freeze | grep -E "dbt|pyspark|duckdb">. What
differs between the two environments, and which single command reproduces CI locally?

ai_prompts.prompt:
Review this workflow for least privilege, secret exposure, supply-chain risk and wasted minutes: <paste ci.yml>.
For each finding: the line, the risk, the fix. Do not suggest paid services.

`actionlint` passes with no findings.
A green run on `main` with the parity summary on the run page.
A PR that failed parity on purpose (link it), then was fixed.
`.github/dependabot.yml`.
Branch protection on your fork's `main`.
`AI_LOG.md` entry.

quiz.q: Why not use `on: push: paths:` to skip CI when only docs change?
options: It is not supported for pull requests
A skipped workflow never reports its checks, so a required check stays "pending" and blocks the PR forever; per-job `if:` with an aggregator job avoids it
quiz.explanation: Always run the workflow, decide per job, and require `ci-ok`, which treats skipped jobs as fine.

quiz.q: What does the `contract` job's `diff -r` of a regenerated fixture prove?
options: The committed fixture is exactly what the seeded generator produces, so nobody hand-edited it to make a test pass
quiz.explanation: Test data is code. If it can drift from its generator, a failing test can be "fixed" by editing the data.

quiz.q: Why does CI install Airflow with a constraints file?
options: Airflow has hundreds of transitive dependencies; the constraints pin all of them to versions tested together, the same as locally and in the Docker image
quiz.explanation: Without pins, a new release of some dependency can break the DAG tests overnight with no change on your side.

quiz.q: The `parity` job runs the full history through both tracks. Why is the fixture not enough?
options: Three days cannot exercise month boundaries, 30-day windows, cohort maturity or late status changes across weeks; the full history can, and the two tracks must agree on all of it
The golden files only cover the full history
quiz.explanation: The fixture is for fast, hand-checkable unit tests; parity on three months is the end-to-end proof.

quiz.q: CI is red, your laptop is green. What is the first thing to compare?
options: Tool versions (Python, Java, dbt, PySpark, DuckDB) and untracked files on your laptop (a `target/`, a `lake/`, a local seed)
quiz.explanation: CI starts from a clean checkout with pinned versions. Most "works on my machine" bugs are a version or a file that exists only on your machine.

quiz.q: Which permission does Pipewright's CI need?
options: `contents: read` (and `pull-requests: read` for the path filter); nothing else, no secrets
quiz.explanation: Least privilege: CI reads code and reports checks. The pipeline's production runs are Airflow's job, not CI's.

Path filters with an aggregator job, and why required checks must always report.

Reproducible test data checked in CI, and full-history parity of two implementations as the merge gate.
Dependabot and actionlint; branch protection with required checks.

phases.title: v1.0: the scheduled pipeline, the dashboard, the AI explainer, Docker
phases.heading: Phase 6 · v1.0: the scheduled pipeline, the dashboard, the AI explainer, Docker
phases.why_md:
Until now the pipeline runs when you type a command. A data product runs **every morning without you**: Airflow
starts it at 06:00 IST, waits for late files, retries what is flaky, never retries a failed check, and the CEO opens a
dashboard that says which day it shows. When a check blocks the publish, the on-call engineer gets an incident note
that says what failed and what to try first. In this phase you build the Streamlit dashboard, the optional AI incident
explainer with guardrails and an offline fallback, the Docker images and Compose stack (non-root, read-only, under
6 GB), an acceptance check that runs all of it in CI, a runbook, and you release **v1.0.0**.
objectives: Build a dashboard that reads only the published warehouse, shows its business date and the five reports, and is tested in CI.
Add an AI feature safely: only aggregate facts go out, the answer is checked by guardrails, and every failure falls back to a deterministic template.
Package every component in small, non-root Docker images with read-only file systems, and wire them with Compose profiles.
Run the Airflow DAG end to end in a container, on Postgres, and read its logs.
Prove the release with one acceptance script (images, pipelines in containers, parity, smoke tests, AI provider down, no secrets in logs).
Write a runbook and release v1.0.0 with a CHANGELOG.

steps.title: The dashboard
steps.content_md:
Remove `"Phase 6 - dashboard"` from the `PENDING` lists. The dashboard (`dashboard/app.py` + `dashboard/data.py`) has
one tab per report plus a *Data health* tab. Rules:
- read `warehouse/pipewright.duckdb` **read-only**, never the build file;
- show "Data as of <business date>" and the age in days at the top; a stale dashboard must say so;
- format money from paise as ₹ with Indian digit grouping (₹3,98,25,047), computed in Python, not in SQL strings;
- keep queries in `data.py` (testable without Streamlit); `app.py` only lays out.
```bash
make install-dashboard && make test-dashboard
make dashboard                       # http://127.0.0.1:18142 on the warehouse from your last `make run`
```
The tests use Streamlit's `AppTest` to render every tab against a small warehouse built from the fixture.

steps.title: The AI incident explainer (optional at runtime, required in tests)
steps.content_md:
Remove `"Phase 6 - AI incident explainer"`. Implement `pipewright/explainer.py`'s `validate` and `explain`:
1. **Facts, not data:** `facts_from(report)` turns the failed checks into numbered facts (`[1] status_accepted
   failed: 41 rows outside the enum, values: lost`). Only these facts are sent: no rows, no customer ids.
2. **Provider:** `AI_PROVIDER=template` (default) never calls anything. `AI_PROVIDER=openai` calls any
   OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`AI_BASE_URL`, `AI_MODEL`, optional `AI_API_KEY`): Ollama locally
   (`http://localhost:11434/v1`), or a free tier. No paid key is ever required.
3. **Guardrails (`validate`):** the answer must cite at least one existing fact `[n]`, contain no number that is not
   in the facts, no URL, no data-changing SQL (`DROP`, `DELETE`, `UPDATE`, ...), and be short. Otherwise → reject.
4. **Fallback:** a timeout, an HTTP error, a missing setting or a rejected answer → the deterministic template, and
   the note says why (`Source: template (provider unavailable: ...)`). The key is never printed or logged.
```bash
.venv/bin/pipewright explain --report contract/fixture/incident-report.json
AI_PROVIDER=openai AI_BASE_URL=http://10.255.255.1:9/v1 AI_MODEL=x AI_TIMEOUT=2 \
  .venv/bin/pipewright explain --report contract/fixture/incident-report.json     # unreachable → template, says why
```
The tests use a local fake LLM (`scripts/fake_llm.py`, modes `good`, `numbers`, `url`, `slow`) that answers well,
invents a number, adds a URL or hangs.

steps.title: Docker images and Compose
steps.content_md:
Read the Dockerfiles (`source/`, `tracks/sql/`, `tracks/pyspark/`, `dashboard/`, `orchestration/`) and
`docker-compose.yml`. What to look for:
- `python:3.12-slim` bases, dependencies installed in one layer **before** the code is copied (fast rebuilds);
- a non-root user (`uid 10001`), `read_only: true`, `tmpfs: /tmp`, `cap_drop: [ALL]`, `no-new-privileges`;
- ports bound to `127.0.0.1` only; HTTPS package mirrors (`DEBIAN_MIRROR` build arg) for networks that block HTTP;
- profiles: default (source + dashboard), `pipeline` (the two pipelines + parity), `airflow` (Postgres + Airflow),
  `ai-test` (the fake LLM); memory limits (Airflow 3 GB, PySpark 2 GB): about 5 GB with everything up.
```bash
cp .env.example .env                     # every variable is optional; defaults are offline
docker compose up -d --build             # source :18140 + dashboard :18142
docker compose --profile pipeline run --rm pipeline-sql run --start 2026-06-01 --end 2026-08-31
docker compose --profile pipeline run --rm pipeline-pyspark run --start 2026-06-01 --end 2026-08-31
docker compose --profile pipeline run --rm parity
```

- a non-root user (`uid 10001`), `read_only: true`, `tmpfs: /tmp`, `cap_drop: [ALL]`, `no-new-privileges`;

quiz.q: Why does the explainer send numbered facts instead of the failing rows?
options: Rows are too long for the model
Facts are aggregates (check ids, counts, safe codes) that cannot leak personal data, and numbering them lets the guardrails check every claim cites a real fact
quiz.explanation: Data minimisation plus verifiability: the model only sees what it needs, and its answer can be checked against what it saw.

quiz.q: The AI provider times out. What does the on-call engineer get?
options: A retry loop until the provider answers
The deterministic template note, which says it is the template and why (provider unavailable)
The last AI note from yesterday
quiz.explanation: The AI is an optional improvement; the template is always available offline and is what the tests and CI rely on.

quiz.q: Why does the dashboard read the published file read-only and never the build file?
options: The build file may be half-built or failed; the published file is complete, checked and swapped in atomically
quiz.explanation: That is the publish gate from Phase 2, seen from the reader's side.

quiz.q: Which container setting limits damage if the dashboard is compromised?
options: A non-root user, `read_only: true`, `cap_drop: [ALL]`, `no-new-privileges`, and a port bound to 127.0.0.1
quiz.explanation: Defence in depth: an attacker who gets code execution cannot write to the image, gain privileges or reach the container from another machine.

quiz.q: Why does `docker-check.sh` grep every log for a fake API key?
options: To prove the key is never printed (in errors, debug output or tracebacks), even when the provider fails
Because the key is needed in logs for debugging
quiz.explanation: A secret that reaches a log reaches every system the logs are shipped to. Test for it like any other requirement.

quiz.q: The DAG's `dq` task has `retries=0`. Why?
options: A failed check is a fact about the data, not a flaky failure; retrying gives the same result and delays the alert
quiz.explanation: Retry transient failures (network, late files); fail fast on deterministic ones and page a human.

phases.heading: Phase 7 · v1.1: incremental models, backfills, schema evolution, monitoring and alerts
phases.why_md:
v1.0 went live on 1 September. On 2 September the 06:00 run was **blocked**: Marketing had launched a new
`influencer` channel and the first customers it acquired failed the `channel_accepted` check. The gate did its job
(the CEO saw 31 August's numbers, clearly labelled), but nobody noticed until the CEO asked at 09:00 why the dashboard
was a day old. Three days later the orders API started sending a new status, `rto` (return to origin: the courier
could not deliver a cash-on-delivery order). On 15 September coupons launched and the ads export gained a column, and
on 21 September the spend file arrived three hours late. This phase is the pipeline's
second month: you version the contract for the new values without breaking v1.0 readers, make the daily build
incremental (and prove it equals a full rebuild), add a backfill command, and add the monitoring that would have paged
someone at 06:45 instead of the CEO at 09:00. You end with a post-mortem and **v1.1.0**.
objectives: Evolve a data contract additively (new enum values, new optional columns), version it, and prove backward compatibility in both directions.
Make fact tables incremental with a lookback window for late updates, and prove incremental = full refresh on every table.
Backfill a past range safely (re-ingest, rebuild only what it touched) without touching later days.
Monitor freshness, volume, the publish SLA and data-quality history; raise alerts to a log and an optional webhook without leaking its URL.
Run a late-file drill and write a blameless post-mortem with actions.

steps.title: Incremental facts, proven equal to a full refresh
steps.content_md:
A full rebuild re-reads every partition every day. Incremental: rebuild only the orders **updated since D − 3 days**
(the `lookback_days` of late status changes), plus lines whose category was `unknown` (a late-arriving product), and
merge them into the previously published facts. A full refresh happens when there is no published warehouse, the
contract version changed, the other track built it, or you pass `--full-refresh`.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt:** make `fct_order_items` and `fct_orders` incremental:
```sql
{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id', incremental_strategy='delete+insert',
          on_schema_change='fail') }}
...
{% if is_incremental() %}
where {{ ist_date('orders.updated_at_utc') }} >= {{ incremental_since() }}      -- var since, or run_date - lookback
   or items.order_id in (select previous.order_id from {{ this }} as previous where previous.category = 'unknown')
{% endif %}
```
`delete+insert` by `order_id` replaces every line of a changed order (a line can disappear). `on_schema_change='fail'`
turns an unplanned column change into a loud error instead of a silent drift. The runner copies the published
warehouse into the build first, so `{{ this }}` is yesterday's facts. dbt unit tests on an incremental model need
`overrides: {macros: {is_incremental: false}}`.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark:** the runner exports the previously published facts to Parquet (`--previous`); `pipeline.facts()`
keeps the previous rows whose `order_id` is **not** in the rebuilt set and unions the rebuilt rows:
```python
changed = silver_orders.where(F.col("updated_at_utc") >= since).select("order_id").union(unknown_ids).distinct()
rebuilt = build_facts(silver.join(changed, "order_id"))
merged = previous.join(changed, "order_id", "left_anti").unionByName(rebuilt)
```
Write Parquet to `<table>.next` and swap, never overwrite the folder you are reading from. Read CSV drops grouped by
header, so 4- and 5-column spend files can be read in one run (the September bug).
<!-- /track -->

Prove it: `make incremental` runs 26-30 September one day at a time (incremental) and compares every gold table with a
`--full-refresh` of the same lake, on both tracks. It must print `MATCH` for all nine tables.

steps.title: Backfills
steps.content_md:
`pipewright backfill --start 2026-09-10 --end 2026-09-12` re-ingests the range (the source may have corrected it) and
rebuilds with `since` = the first day, so every order touched in the range is rebuilt; later days are untouched and the
published date does not move backwards. Every run (daily, backfill, blocked, failed) is recorded in `ops.run_log`.

steps.title: Monitoring and alerts
steps.content_md:
Implement `pipewright monitor --date D [--now ISO]` from the contract's `monitoring:` section:
- **freshness:** file drops by 05:00 IST (payments `error`, spend and catalogue `warn`); API data in the lake by 06:15;
- **volume:** the day's rows between 0.5× and 2× the median of the previous 7 days;
- **SLA:** D published by 06:30 IST; **dq:** the latest report's blocking failures.
Results go to `ops.duckdb` (rewritten copy-and-replace so the dashboard can read it) and every alert to
`warehouse/reports/alerts.jsonl`; alerts at or above `ALERT_MIN_SEVERITY` (default `error`) are POSTed to `ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL`
if set. The URL is a secret: never log it, and a failing webhook never fails the pipeline. Add a `monitor` task at the
end of the daily DAG (`trigger_rule=ALL_DONE`, so it runs even when publishing failed) and a `pipewright_watch` DAG at
05:45 and 06:45 IST. Add a *Data health* section to the dashboard.

steps.title: The late-file drill and backward compatibility
steps.content_md:
```bash
make drill        # replays 21 Sep: 05:45 warn (spend missing) → 06:00 run waits (exit 3) → 06:45 errors (SLA, orders)
                  # → the file arrives → incremental publish → monitor green
make backcompat OLD=../v1.0.0     # git worktree add ../v1.0.0 v1.0.0 first
```
Backcompat checks three things: **A** the v1.1 pipeline on v1.0 data reproduces the v1.0 golden reports (old data, new
code); **B** the v1.0 dashboard renders a v1.1 warehouse (new data, old reader); **C** the v1.0 pipeline on v1.1 data
refuses to publish and the last good day stays (the September incident, contained by the gate). Add `make incremental`,
`make drill` and the backcompat check to CI (the `v11` job, with `fetch-depth: 0` for the tag), finish the post-mortem,
add a monitoring section to the runbook, CHANGELOG `1.1.0`, tag `v1.1.0`.

quiz.q: Why is adding `rto` to the order statuses a minor (1.1.0) and not a patch or major change?
options: It is additive: existing values, columns and meanings stay, so old readers keep working; but numbers can change (rto orders stop counting), so it is more than a patch; nothing is removed or renamed, so it is not major
Versions do not matter for data
quiz.explanation: Version the contract like an API. Additive = minor; removing, renaming or changing a meaning = major, with a migration plan.

quiz.q: Why does the incremental build rebuild orders updated in the last 3 days instead of only yesterday's?
options: Status changes and corrections can arrive late; the lookback re-processes every order that may have changed since the last builds, so the facts stay equal to a full rebuild
quiz.explanation: Incremental logic is a promise: "same result as a full rebuild, cheaper". The lookback window (and the unknown-category rule) is what keeps it; `make incremental` checks it.

quiz.q: Why `delete+insert` by `order_id` rather than `merge` by `(order_id, line_number)`?
options: An updated order can lose a line; replacing all lines of each changed order removes it, while a per-line merge would keep the stale line
quiz.explanation: Choose the incremental grain from how the source changes: here the order is the unit of change.

quiz.q: The spend file is late. At 05:45 the monitor raises a `warn`; at 06:45 an `error`. Why two severities?
options: Before the deadline it is a heads-up (the file may still arrive); after the SLA it is an incident that needs a human, and only that should page
quiz.explanation: Alert on symptoms that matter, at the time they matter. Too many pages train people to ignore them.

quiz.q: Why must the webhook URL never appear in logs?
options: Incoming-webhook URLs contain a secret token: anyone with the URL can post to the channel
quiz.explanation: Treat it like a password. Log "webhook delivery failed (HTTP 500)" without the URL, and never let a failed alert fail the pipeline.

quiz.q: Backcompat check C runs the v1.0 pipeline on v1.1 data and expects it to FAIL. Why is that a pass?
options: It is a bug in the check
Old code meeting new values must refuse to publish rather than publish wrong numbers; the check proves the gate still contains the incident and the last good day stays visible
quiz.explanation: Forward compatibility of old code is not always possible; failing safe is the requirement. Check C turns the September incident into a regression test.

recap: Contract versioning and additive schema evolution, with backward-compatibility checks in both directions.
Incremental models with a lookback for late data, and full-refresh equality as their test.
Safe backfills and a run log.
Monitoring of freshness, volume, SLA and data quality; alerting with severities and secret-safe webhooks.
Drills and blameless post-mortems as part of operating a pipeline.

phases.title: Retrospective and portfolio
phases.heading: Phase 8 · Retrospective and portfolio
phases.why_md:
A project you cannot explain in two minutes does not exist for a hiring manager. And a project you do not reflect
on teaches you half of what it could. In this phase you look back at nine phases with numbers (what took longest,
what broke, what the tests caught, where AI helped and where it misled you), write a retrospective, turn the README
into a case study a reviewer can read in three minutes, and prepare the story of the September incident, the decision
you are proudest of and the one you would change.

legacy_import.title: Pipewright: End-to-End Data Pipeline for a CEO Dashboard
legacy_import.description: BazaarBox, a direct-to-consumer home & kitchen brand, wants one dashboard that is correct by 06:30 IST every day: revenue by category and region, CAC by channel, Prime membership MRR, the top 10 products of the last 30 days and 30-day cohort retention. Over nine phases you build the pipeline behind it like a data engineering team: write requirements with SLAs and acceptance criteria, design the architecture, the bronze/silver/gold layers, a data contract and five ADRs (including why Airbyte, a Spark cluster and Metabase were swapped for lighter tools), then build it test-first. A seeded, offline copy of BazaarBox's systems (an orders and customers API with bearer tokens, cursor pagination, updated_at windows and injected 429/503 faults, plus daily payment, ad-spend and catalogue file drops) comes with real-world defects: mixed time zones, re-delivered orders, duplicate payment events, rupee amounts as text, city spellings, test orders and PII. You write idempotent ingestion into immutable lake partitions, silver and gold models in dbt (SQL track) or PySpark (Python track) whose gold tables must equal the golden files and each other row by row, declarative data-quality checks with severities and a publish gate built on an atomic swap, dbt data and unit tests, and a GitHub Actions pipeline that runs dbt build on a fixture and both tracks on the full history. v1.0.0 adds an Airflow 3 schedule, a Streamlit dashboard, an optional AI incident explainer with guardrails and an offline fallback, and a hardened Docker Compose stack under 6 GB of RAM. Then the pipeline meets its second month: a new channel and a new order status block publishing, coupons change the schema, and a partner file arrives late. You version the contract additively, make the facts incremental and prove them equal to a full refresh, add backfills, freshness, volume and SLA monitoring with alerts, prove backward compatibility with v1.0, and write a blameless post-mortem (v1.1.0). Everything runs on a laptop with no paid service and no API key.
legacy_import.tech_stack: SQL, PySpark, Python, dbt, DuckDB, PySpark, Apache Airflow, Streamlit, Docker, PostgreSQL, GitHub Actions

steps.title: Phase 0 · Setup, the brief and the sources
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
A dashboard nobody can rebuild is a screenshot with a refresh button. Data teams start where engineers start: a
repository that installs with one command, source data whose origin you can prove, tests that say what "right"
means, and a log of how AI helped. In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, read the brief, meet
BazaarBox's sources (an API and three file drops) and their defects, run the starter, meet the pending tests and
the contract that will guide you, open your first pull request and start your `AI_LOG.md`. You will not write a
single transformation yet, on purpose: first you learn who needs which number, when, and what the sources can and
cannot tell you.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
- Pick a track (SQL · dbt or Python · PySpark), install the toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux, and run `make lint test`.
- Explain the brief in two sentences: who needs which five numbers, by when, and what a wrong number costs.
