- Generate the source data, prove it is exactly the published one (the manifest check), call the API stub with a token and list three defects you can see in the raw records, plus the two fields that must never reach the lake.
- Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 0.1 · Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/end-to-end-data-pipeline` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**.
   The `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/end-to-end-data-pipeline.git
   cd end-to-end-data-pipeline
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/end-to-end-data-pipeline.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/end-to-end-data-pipeline`), not under `/mnt/c`.

### Step 0.2 · Install the tools for ONE track
Every track needs Git, `make` and Python 3.12: ingestion, the checks, the runner, the DAG and the dashboard are
shared Python. Run the doctor script; it tells you exactly what is missing:
```bash
scripts/doctor.sh
make setup            # .venv with the shared package and both tracks' pinned tools
```
`make setup` installs both tracks so you can run the parity check later; you will only *write* code in one.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt track:** dbt-core 1.12 with the DuckDB adapter. DuckDB is an in-process analytical database: no
server, the warehouse is one file, and it reads the lake's JSONL and CSV files directly. Your silver and gold
models are SQL files in `tracks/sql/models`; dbt builds them in dependency order, runs their tests and enforces
the column contracts.
```bash
.venv/bin/dbt --version                         # Core 1.12.x, duckdb 1.11.x
cd tracks/sql && ../../.venv/bin/dbt parse --profiles-dir .   # the project loads (no data needed)
```
Optional: the DuckDB CLI (`brew install duckdb`, or the binary from duckdb.org) to explore files by hand.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark track:** PySpark 4.2 in **local mode**: the Spark engine runs inside one JVM on your laptop, no
cluster. Your silver and gold models are DataFrame functions in `tracks/pyspark/pipewright_spark`; the gold
tables are written as Parquet and registered in the same DuckDB warehouse, so the checks and the dashboard do not
care which track built them. Spark needs Java 17 or 21:
```bash
java -version                                   # 17 or 21
.venv/bin/python -c "from pyspark.sql import SparkSession as S; s = S.builder.master('local[1]').getOrCreate(); print(s.version); s.stop()"
```
If Spark complains about the host name, set `export SPARK_LOCAL_IP=127.0.0.1`.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 0.3 · Read the brief
Read the top of `README.md` (the situation) and `contract/transform-spec.md` §1 (conventions). Write down, in your
own words: **who needs which number, how often, by what time, and what each kind of wrong number costs** (a revenue
figure that double-counts a duplicated payment? a CAC computed with test accounts? yesterday's dashboard shown as
today's?). Phase 1 turns your notes into requirements.

### Step 0.4 · Meet the sources
Generate the source data and check it is byte-for-byte the published one, then start the API stub:
```bash
make source            # generate → check against contract/source-manifest-1.0.json → serve on 127.0.0.1:18140
```
In a second terminal, look at the data the way an engineer does, from the outside:
```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18140/health
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:18140/v1/orders          # 401: a token is required
curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer bazaarbox-dev-token' \
  'http://127.0.0.1:18140/v1/orders?updated_since=2026-06-01T00:00:00%2B05:30&updated_before=2026-06-02T00:00:00%2B05:30&limit=3' \
  | python3 -m json.tool | head -60
head -3 source-data/drops/marketing_spend/spend_2026-06-01.csv
head -2 source-data/drops/payments/payments_2026-06-01.jsonl
cut -d, -f3 source-data/drops/products/products_2026-06-01.csv | sort | uniq -c
```
Read `source/README.md`. Then note three defects you can see without any code (two time-zone formats? amounts as
text with a rupee sign? the same payment event twice? a category with a leading space?), and find the two fields
the contract says must be dropped before anything is written (`contract/data-contract.yaml`, `pii_drop`).

### Step 0.5 · Run the checks and meet the pending tests and the contract
```bash
make lint test
```
All the tests are **skipped**. They are *pending*: the complete test suite is already written and switched off in
one `PENDING` list per suite:

| Suite | Pending list |
|---|---|
| shared package | `pipewright/tests/conftest.py` |
| SQL · dbt | `tracks/sql/pytests/conftest.py` |
| Python · PySpark | `tracks/pyspark/tests/conftest.py` |
| Airflow DAG | `orchestration/tests/conftest.py` |

Each entry names a milestone ("Phase 3 M2 - silver (staging) models"). In Phase 3 you delete one entry at a time,
watch the tests go red, and make them green.

Now open the files of `contract/` that make "right" precise (`contract/README.md` lists them all):
- `data-contract.yaml`: what each source must send, the enums, every gold table's columns and types, and the
  data-quality checks with their severities;
- `transform-spec.md`: every rule in words: parsing, silver, gold, the five reports;
- `fixture/source/` + `golden/fixture/`: three days of source data and the gold tables they must produce, small
  enough to check by hand; `golden/v1.0/`: the reference reports for the full three months.

### Step 0.6 · Your first pull request
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant explained a `java` / `dbt` / `pip` error during the
   install and how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab. Forks have Actions switched off until you click **"I understand my workflows, go ahead
   and enable them"**. CI runs lint + unit tests for the shared package and both tracks. Wait for green, fill in the
   PR template and merge.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Fix my toolchain install
```text
I'm on <Windows 11 + WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 | macOS 15 | Ubuntu 24.04>. I want to run a project that needs Python 3.12
with a virtual environment, <dbt-core 1.12 with dbt-duckdb | PySpark 4.2 in local mode with Java 21>, make and
shellcheck. Here is the output of scripts/doctor.sh: <paste output>. Give me the exact commands to install what is
missing, explain each one in one line, and tell me how to verify each install.
```
**Verify the output by:** running each verification command, re-running `scripts/doctor.sh` until every required
line is green, and checking any download URL against the official site (python.org, adoptium.net, docs.getdbt.com,
spark.apache.org, docs.docker.com). Never pipe an unknown URL into `bash`.

### Prompt 2: Restate the brief as requirements
```text
Here is a stakeholder brief: <paste the "situation" paragraph of README.md>. Restate it as: (1) who needs which
number, at which grain, how often and by what time, (2) for each of the five reports, the questions I must ask
before I can define it exactly (which orders count as revenue? which day does an order belong to?), (3) three ways
the dashboard could show a plausible but wrong number, (4) what "fresh" and "correct" should mean, measurably.
Do not invent numbers or facts that are not in the brief.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking every claim against the brief (assistants add details that are not there, such
as a revenue target or a data warehouse BazaarBox does not have), and keeping at least one failure mode about
*time* (a time zone, a late update, a late file). `contract/transform-spec.md` §1 answers several of the questions.

### Prompt 3: Read a source like a data engineer
```text
Here are 3 records from a REST API of an e-commerce company and the header plus 5 rows of two daily CSV files:
<paste the curl output and the head of the spend and products files>. List every data-quality problem you can see
or suspect, how you would detect each one in code, which fields look like personal data, and what you would ask
the source owner. Do not write any transformation yet.
```
**Verify the output by:** finding each problem in the real data with `grep`, `cut | sort | uniq -c` or a quick
DuckDB query (an assistant may "see" problems that are not in your sample), and comparing your list with
`contract/transform-spec.md` §2-§3. These records are synthetic; with real customer data you would paste schemas
and aggregates only, never rows with emails or phone numbers.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] Your fork contains the `solution` branch and the `phase-*` tags (`git tag -l` shows them).
- [ ] `make lint test` passes locally (all tests skipped).
- [ ] `make source` says the generated files are identical to the manifest, and you called the API with a token.
- [ ] A note (in your PR description or `AI_LOG.md`): the five reports and their deadline, three source defects, and the two PII fields.
- [ ] A merged PR with a green CI run.
- [ ] `AI_LOG.md` has its first entry.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
- [ ] Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
- [x] Otherwise the `solution` branch and the phase tags are missing from your fork
- [ ] Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
- [ ] Otherwise the source data is not copied
> **Answer:** Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch; without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

### Q2. Why does `make source` check the generated files against `contract/source-manifest-1.0.json`?
- [ ] To make generation faster
- [ ] To encrypt the source data
- [x] To prove your source data is byte-for-byte the data the golden tables were computed from, so a difference in your numbers is a bug in your code, not different input
- [ ] Because Git cannot store JSONL files
> **Answer:** The manifest lists the sha256 of every generated file. Same seed, same bytes. If the check fails, nothing downstream can be compared with the golden tables.

### Q3. The orders API returns an order on 1 June and the same order again on 4 June. What happened?
- [ ] The API has a bug and returns duplicates
- [x] The order changed (e.g. it was delivered or cancelled), so its `updated_at` moved into a later extraction window; the pipeline must keep the latest version
- [ ] A customer placed the same order twice
- [ ] The pagination cursor was reused
> **Answer:** Incremental extraction by `updated_at` sees every change of a record, so the same key appears in several daily partitions. Silver keeps the latest version per key (`transform-spec.md` §3.1). Counting both would double the revenue.

### Q4. Why are all tests skipped in the starter?
- [ ] They are flaky
- [ ] CI is too slow to run them
- [x] They describe behaviour you build in Phases 3-6 and are switched on one milestone at a time
- [ ] They only run on the solution branch
> **Answer:** The full suite is written up-front (test-first). Deleting a line from a `PENDING` list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

### Q5. Which fields must never reach the lake?
- [ ] `order_id` and `customer_id`
- [x] The customer's `email` and `phone`
- [ ] `ship_city`
- [ ] Every timestamp
> **Answer:** The contract's `pii_drop` lists them for the customers source. None of the five reports needs them, so the safest place to drop them is before the first byte is written: data you never store cannot leak.

### Q6. Which of these may you paste into an AI prompt for this project?
- [ ] Your `.env` file with an API key
- [ ] 500 customer records with emails and phone numbers
- [x] Column names, your own code, an error message and aggregate counts
- [ ] Another student's dbt project
> **Answer:** Secrets and row-level personal data never go into prompts. The BazaarBox data is synthetic, but practise the habit you need at work: schemas, code and aggregates, not rows.

## 7. What you learned
- A reproducible local environment for one track, checked by `scripts/doctor.sh` and `make lint test`.
- The difference between `origin` (your fork) and `upstream` (the course repo), and why tags matter.
- The brief as five numbers with a deadline, and the ways a dashboard can be plausible and wrong.
- BazaarBox's sources from the outside: a paginated, authenticated API with incremental windows and three file drops, each with its defects.
- The contract (data contract, transformation spec, fixture, golden tables, manifest) that defines "right".
- The PR + CI loop and the habit of logging AI assistance without leaking secrets or rows.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
# Start Phase 1 from the reference end of Phase 0:
git switch -c my-phase-1 phase-0-end
# See what the reference changed in this phase:
git diff main phase-0-end --stat
```

steps.title: Phase 1 · Requirements: the five reports, SLAs and acceptance criteria
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
"Revenue by region" sounds like a requirement. It is not one until you know which orders count (placed? paid?
delivered? not cancelled? not test orders?), which day an order belongs to (the customer's day in India, or the
server's day in UTC?), what happens when an order is cancelled a week later, and by what time the number must be
right. Most dashboard disputes are not bugs in SQL; they are two people with two definitions. In this phase you
turn the CEO's five questions into **written, testable definitions**, service levels for freshness and
correctness, and user stories with acceptance criteria that include bad and late data. Everything you build in
Phases 3-7 is checked against this document.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Name the stakeholders, the decision each one makes with the dashboard, and how often.
- Define each of the five reports exactly: grain, measures, filters, the day an event belongs to, and an example row.
- Write non-functional requirements with a measure and a test: freshness (by 06:30 IST), correctness (reconciliation), idempotency, privacy, footprint.
- Write user stories with Given / When / Then acceptance criteria, including a late update, a duplicate event and a missing file.
- Say what is out of scope for v1.0 and why.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 1.1 · Stakeholders and their decisions
Copy `spec/requirements-template.md` to `spec/requirements.md`. Fill in §1: for the CEO, the Head of Marketing,
the Head of Category and Finance, write the decision they make with the dashboard ("move ad budget between
channels at the start of each month") and which report serves it. A report nobody decides with is a candidate
for "out of scope".

### Step 1.2 · Define the five reports precisely
For each report write: the question, the grain (one row per what?), every measure as a formula, the filters, the
date rule, and one example row you compute by hand from `contract/fixture/source`. Decide, and write down:
- Which order statuses count as revenue, and what happens to revenue when an order is cancelled or returned later?
- Which **calendar** decides the day: an order placed at 23:50 IST on 1 June is `2026-06-01T18:20:00Z`. Which day is it?
- Money: rupees with decimals, or integer paise? Why does it matter when you sum 18,000 order lines?
- CAC: spend divided by which customers? Test accounts? Customers whose channel is unknown? A month with no new customers?
- Prime MRR: how does an annual plan count? When does a cancelled subscription stop counting?
- Top 10: the last 30 days up to which date? Ties?
- Retention: "came back within 30 days" from which event? What about customers who signed up 10 days ago?

Compare your answers with `contract/transform-spec.md` §1 and §5 **after** you have written them. Where you
disagree, write down why: a good spec records the trade-off, not just the rule.

### Step 1.3 · Non-functional requirements (the SLAs)
Fill in §4 with a measure and a test for each:
- **Freshness:** yesterday's (IST) numbers are published by 06:30 IST; the dashboard always shows the business date
  it is showing.
- **Correctness:** every report reconciles to the order lines; a failed blocking check means the previous day stays
  published (a stale number is better than a wrong one).
- **Idempotency:** running the same day twice gives the same tables; re-running a past day replaces it.
- **Privacy:** no email or phone in the lake, the warehouse, the logs or any prompt.
- **Footprint:** runs on an 8 GB laptop and in free CI; no paid service.

### Step 1.4 · User stories with acceptance criteria
Write at least six stories in §3, each with Given / When / Then. At least three must be about **bad or late data**:
```text
Given an order placed on 2026-06-01 and cancelled on 2026-06-04
When the pipeline runs for 2026-06-04
Then the order no longer counts in the revenue of 2026-06-01, and the change is visible on the 2026-06-05 dashboard
```
Other good candidates: the payments file for a day is missing at 06:00; the same payment event arrives twice; a new
order status appears that the contract does not know; the API answers 429 for a minute.

### Step 1.5 · Sources, scope and open questions
Fill in §5 (what each source sends, when, and what can go wrong, from your Phase 0 notes), §6 (out of scope for
v1.0: e.g. real-time numbers, forecasting, per-customer views) and §7 (questions you would ask the CEO). Commit:
```bash
git switch -c docs/phase-1-requirements
git add spec/requirements.md AI_LOG.md
git commit -m "docs(spec): requirements for the five reports, SLAs and acceptance criteria"
```

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt track:** add one line per report to your requirements: the gold model that will serve it
(`mart_revenue_daily`, ...). In dbt, the requirement becomes the model's `description` and its tests in Phase 4;
write the definitions so that you can paste them there.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark track:** add one line per report: the function in `pipewright_spark/gold.py` that will build it.
Write each definition so that it can become the function's docstring, and note which rule needs a window
function (latest version per key, ranking) and which a join.
<!-- /track -->

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Find the ambiguities in a metric definition
```text
Here is my definition of a business metric for an e-commerce dashboard: <paste one report from your
requirements.md>. Act as a sceptical analytics engineer. List every ambiguity that would let two engineers
compute different numbers from the same data (time zones, statuses, late updates, duplicates, test data, ties,
empty periods, rounding). For each, propose a precise rule and say what it costs. Do not compute anything.
```
**Verify the output by:** turning each accepted rule into an example on the fixture (`contract/fixture/source`) and
computing the expected value by hand, and comparing with `contract/transform-spec.md`. Reject rules that need data
BazaarBox does not have.

### Prompt 2: Turn a requirement into acceptance criteria
```text
Requirement: <paste one user story>. Write 3-5 acceptance criteria in Given / When / Then form. At least two must
cover bad or late data (a duplicate, a late status change, a missing file, an unknown value). Each criterion must be
testable with a small fixture; say what the fixture contains.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking each criterion is observable from outside (a table value, an exit code, a file),
that none contradicts your report definitions, and that you could write the fixture in under 10 rows.

### Prompt 3: Challenge my SLAs
```text
My data pipeline must publish yesterday's numbers by 06:30 IST. Sources: an API (available all night) and three
files dropped by partners "around 05:00 IST". Here are my non-functional requirements: <paste §4>. What could make
me miss the SLA, what should happen when a file is late, and how would I measure freshness and correctness in
production? Keep it to the decisions I need to make now.
```
**Verify the output by:** making sure every proposal has a measure and an owner, that "what happens when a file is
late" is a decision (wait, publish partial, keep yesterday) and not a hope, and that nothing requires a paid tool.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `spec/requirements.md` with all seven sections filled in.
- [ ] An exact definition of each of the five reports, with one hand-computed example row from the fixture.
- [ ] Non-functional requirements with a measure and a test each (freshness, correctness, idempotency, privacy, footprint).
- [ ] At least six user stories with acceptance criteria, three of them about bad or late data.
- [ ] An `AI_LOG.md` entry about a definition the AI helped you sharpen (and one suggestion you rejected).

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. An order is placed at 23:50 IST on 1 June. Its timestamp is `2026-06-01T18:20:00Z`. On which business day does it count?
- [x] 1 June: business dates are IST calendar days
- [ ] 2 June, because UTC is the standard
- [ ] It depends on the server's time zone
- [ ] Neither: orders near midnight are excluded
> **Answer:** The contract fixes the calendar (`timezone: Asia/Kolkata`). Here the UTC date happens to be the same, but an order at 00:20 IST on 2 June is `2026-06-01T18:50:00Z`: grouping by the UTC date puts it on the wrong day. Never let the machine's time zone decide.

### Q2. Why does the contract store money as integer paise?
- [ ] Paise use less disk space
- [x] Floating-point sums of thousands of rupee amounts drift by fractions of a paisa, so two correct pipelines can disagree; integers sum exactly
- [ ] The dashboard cannot show decimals
- [ ] Indian law requires it
> **Answer:** `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` in floating point. With integers, the SQL and PySpark tracks produce the same totals to the paisa, and the reconciliation checks can demand exact equality.

### Q3. A blocking data-quality check fails at 06:05. What should the CEO see at 06:30?
- [ ] The new numbers with a warning banner
- [ ] An empty dashboard
- [x] Yesterday's last good numbers, clearly labelled with their business date, while the team investigates
- [ ] Whatever the pipeline produced; checks are only advisory
> **Answer:** A stale number that says it is stale is better than a wrong number that looks fresh. That is the publish gate you build in Phases 3-4.

### Q4. Which acceptance criterion is testable?
- [ ] "The dashboard is accurate"
- [ ] "Late data is handled gracefully"
- [x] "Given a payment event delivered twice, when the day is processed, then it is counted once in MRR"
- [ ] "The pipeline is fast"
> **Answer:** A testable criterion names the input, the action and an observable result. The other three are wishes until someone defines accurate, gracefully and fast.

### Q5. What belongs in "out of scope for v1.0"?
- [ ] Anything difficult
- [x] Things a stakeholder might expect but v1.0 deliberately does not do (e.g. intraday numbers), with the reason, so the expectation is managed early
- [ ] The tests
- [ ] The five reports
> **Answer:** Writing scope down prevents the worst kind of surprise: the one at the demo. It also gives v1.1 (Phase 7) a backlog.

### Q6. Your assistant suggests "count revenue when the payment is captured" instead of by order status. What do you do?
- [ ] Accept it: payments are more accurate
- [x] Treat it as a design question: check it against the brief and the sources (cash-on-delivery orders have no captured payment until delivery), and record the decision and its trade-off
- [ ] Reject it: AI suggestions are never right
- [ ] Implement both and let the CEO pick a number
> **Answer:** It may be a good idea, but it changes the meaning of the number and depends on data you have not checked. A definition change is a stakeholder decision, written down, not an implementation detail.

## 7. What you learned
- A metric is not defined until its grain, filters, calendar, money unit and late-data behaviour are.
- Service levels for a data product: freshness, correctness, idempotency, privacy, footprint, each with a measure.
- Acceptance criteria that include bad and late data, testable on a small fixture.
- Scope as a tool for managing expectations, and open questions as part of the deliverable.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-2 phase-1-end
git show phase-1-end:spec/requirements.md | less      # the reference requirements (after writing yours)
```

steps.title: Phase 2 · Design: architecture, the data contract, layers and ADRs
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
The old version of this project started with a tool list: Airbyte, Delta Lake, a Spark cluster, dbt, Airflow,
Metabase, Postgres. Together they need more than 16 GB of RAM, and none of them answers the questions that decide
whether the dashboard is right: where does each record land, can a day be re-run without duplicates, what happens
when a check fails, who may read a half-built table? Design is answering those questions **before** the code, and
choosing tools that fit the answers and the laptop. In this phase you draw the architecture, define the layers and
their contracts, read the data contract that pins every source and gold table, and record the five decisions that
shape the project as Architecture Decision Records (ADRs).

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Draw the pipeline: sources → ingestion → lake (bronze) → silver → gold → checks → publish → dashboard, and say what each step guarantees.
- Explain bronze / silver / gold (the "medallion" layers): grain, mutability, who writes and who reads each.
- Design idempotent ingestion: extraction windows, cursors, retries, partition replacement, manifests, PII handling.
- Design a publish gate so the dashboard never reads a half-built or failed build.
- Read `contract/data-contract.yaml` and say what each section enforces.
- Justify every tool choice against the requirements and an 8 GB RAM budget, and write five ADRs.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 2.1 · Draw the architecture
Copy `spec/design-template.md` to `spec/design.md` and draw §1 (Mermaid renders on GitHub):
```text
flowchart LR
  API[orders/customers API] --> ING[ingest]
  DROPS[file drops] --> ING
  ING --> BRONZE[(lake: raw, immutable)]
  BRONZE --> SILVER[silver: one clean row per entity]
  SILVER --> GOLD[gold: facts, dims, 5 reports]
  GOLD --> DQ{checks}
  DQ -- pass --> PUB[(published warehouse)]
  DQ -- fail --> INC[incident report]
  PUB --> DASH[dashboard]
```
For each box write one paragraph: input, output, the guarantee it gives the next box.

### Step 2.2 · Layers and their contracts
Fill in §2. Think about each row: **bronze** keeps every delivery exactly as received (minus PII), partitioned by
delivery date, never edited; silver and gold are always rebuilt from it, so a fixed rule fixes history. **Silver**
has one clean row per business entity (the latest order version, one row per payment event). **Gold** has the
facts, dimensions and the five reports, with the exact columns of the contract. Who may read silver? (Only gold
models.) Who may read gold? (Only through the published warehouse.)

### Step 2.3 · Ingestion that can be re-run
Fill in §3. Decide and justify:
- The extraction window for day D: `[D 00:00 IST, D+1 00:00 IST)` on `updated_at`, half-open, so no record is in two
  windows of the same run and none is missed at midnight.
- Pagination (follow `next_cursor`), retries (429/503 with exponential backoff and jitter, honour `Retry-After`;
  never retry a 401), a timeout on every request.
- Writing: the day's partition is written to a temporary directory and swapped in whole; re-running D replaces it.
  A manifest records what was loaded (counts, sha256, contract version).
- Bad records: rows missing a required field go to `lake/quarantine/` with the reason, not into bronze, and are counted.
- PII: `email` and `phone` are dropped before the first byte is written.

### Step 2.4 · Read the data contract
Open `contract/data-contract.yaml` and annotate (in your design) what each section enforces:

| Section | Enforced by | When it fails |
|---|---|---|
| `sources` (required fields, primary key, `pii_drop`) | ingestion | the record is quarantined; PII never lands |
| `enums` | `accepted_values` checks, dbt tests | the build is not published |
| `gold` (columns, types, order) | dbt model contracts / PySpark `enforce()` | the build fails before it is checked |
| `checks` (severity `error`/`warn`) | `pipewright dq` | `error`: not published; `warn`: published, reported |

Then read `contract/transform-spec.md` once end to end and mark the three rules you think are easiest to get wrong.

### Step 2.5 · The publish gate
Fill in §5. The dashboard reads `warehouse/pipewright.duckdb`. Every run builds into a **separate build file**,
runs the checks on it, records the verdict in the build itself (`ops.build_info`), and only then swaps the build
into place with one atomic rename. A crash, a failed check or a half-written table can therefore never reach the
dashboard: it keeps the last good build, which knows its own business date.

### Step 2.6 · Tools and footprint
Fill in §7. For each tool of the old design, decide keep / replace and why, with the RAM it needs on a laptop.
Then compare with the reference decisions (after writing yours): `git show phase-2-end:spec/design.md`.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt track:** design the dbt project in §4: `models/staging` (one model per source, reading the lake files
through the `lake_glob()` macro, never the API; materialized as tables so the published file is self-contained), `models/gold` (tables, with `contract: {enforced: true}` so the
column names and types of `data-contract.yaml` are checked at build time), seeds (`city_map`), and where the tests
will go (generic tests in YAML, singular tests in `tests/`, unit tests for the trickiest rules). Note why the
models must filter `dt <= run_date` (a backfill must never see the future).
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark track:** design the package in §4: `bronze.py` (read the lake with explicit schemas, never
inferred), `parsing.py` (pure column expressions: time zones, paise), `staging.py` (silver), `gold.py` (facts,
dims, reports), `pipeline.py` (`enforce()` the contract's column types, write Parquet, register the tables in the
DuckDB warehouse). Note why local mode (`local[2]`) with a 1 GB driver is enough for this data and how you will keep Spark's
session time zone from changing your dates (`spark.sql.session.timeZone=UTC`, parse offsets yourself).
<!-- /track -->

### Step 2.7 · Write five ADRs
Use `spec/adr/0000-template.md`. One decision per file, 1/2 page each:
1. Where the data lives (a lake of files + an embedded warehouse vs a lakehouse table format on a cluster).
2. How data is ingested (a connector platform vs a small ingestion package you can read and test).
3. How many ways the transformations are written, and how you know they agree.
4. How a build becomes visible (the publish gate).
5. How the pipeline is scheduled (an orchestrator calling one CLI vs an orchestrator that *is* the code).
Commit `spec/design.md` and `spec/adr/000{1..5}-*.md`.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Review my architecture for failure modes
```text
Here is the architecture of a daily batch pipeline: <paste spec/design.md §1-§3>. Sources: a paginated REST API
with updated_at windows and three daily file drops. Walk through these failures one by one and tell me what my
design does in each case, and where it is unclear: (1) the job crashes halfway through writing a partition,
(2) the same day is run twice, (3) an order changes status three days later, (4) a file arrives 3 hours late,
(5) a new enum value appears, (6) the API rate-limits for two minutes. Do not propose new tools.
```
**Verify the output by:** finding, for each failure, the exact sentence in your design that handles it (if there is
none, the AI found a gap; add it), and rejecting answers that rely on a tool or service you did not choose.

### Prompt 2: Argue the other side of a tool decision
```text
I am choosing between <Airbyte | a small Python ingestion package> for ingesting one REST API and three daily
files on an 8 GB laptop, for a teaching project that must run offline. Give the strongest case FOR the option I
rejected, then the costs of each option (RAM, moving parts, what a learner can read and test, what happens at 100x
the data). Be concrete; no marketing language.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking RAM and container-count claims against the tools' official docs (they change
between versions), and making sure your ADR's "Consequences" section lists the best counter-argument honestly.

### Prompt 3: Draft an ADR from my notes
```text
Context notes: <paste your bullet points for one decision>. Write an ADR with sections Context, Options considered
(at least 3), Decision, Consequences (positive and negative). Keep it under 300 words. Use only facts from my notes;
mark anything you had to assume with [ASSUMPTION].
```
**Verify the output by:** removing or confirming every [ASSUMPTION], checking each option was really considered,
and making sure the decision can be tested (e.g. "a crash during publish leaves the old warehouse readable" is a test
you will write in Phase 3).

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `spec/design.md` with the architecture diagram and all eight sections.
- [ ] A layer table (bronze / silver / gold) with grain, mutability, writers and readers.
- [ ] An ingestion design that explains windows, retries, idempotent partition writes, quarantine and PII handling.
- [ ] The publish gate described so that a crash at any point leaves the dashboard on the last good build.
- [ ] Five ADRs in `spec/adr/`.
- [ ] An `AI_LOG.md` entry, including one AI suggestion you rejected and why.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why is the bronze layer immutable and partitioned by delivery date?
- [ ] Because files are cheaper than tables
- [x] So silver and gold can always be rebuilt from exactly what was received; a fixed rule fixes history, and re-running a day replaces only that day's partition
- [ ] Because dbt cannot update files
- [ ] To save memory
> **Answer:** If bronze were edited in place you could never reproduce yesterday's numbers or replay a bug fix over history. Partitioning by delivery date makes a re-run replace one partition, never append duplicates.

### Q2. Why is the API extraction window half-open, `[D 00:00 IST, D+1 00:00 IST)`?
- [ ] It is faster
- [x] So every instant belongs to exactly one window: a record updated exactly at midnight is loaded once, not twice or never
- [ ] Because the API requires it
- [ ] To skip test orders
> **Answer:** Closed windows `[a, b]` double-load records at the boundary; open ones lose them. Half-open windows tile the time line exactly.

### Q3. What is the purpose of building into a separate file and swapping it in with one rename?
- [ ] Renames are faster than writes
- [ ] To keep a backup
- [x] The dashboard can only ever see a complete build that passed its checks; a crash or a failed check leaves the last good warehouse in place
- [ ] DuckDB cannot write to an open file
> **Answer:** `os.replace` on the same file system is atomic: readers see either the old file or the new one, never a half-written one. The checks run before the swap, so a failed build is never visible.

### Q4. Why did the design replace Airbyte with a small ingestion package?
- [ ] Airbyte cannot read REST APIs
- [x] For one API and three files, a platform needing several GB of RAM and many containers hides the very ideas the project teaches (windows, cursors, retries, idempotency); a few hundred lines of tested Python show them and run on any laptop
- [ ] Airbyte is not open source
- [ ] Python is faster than Airbyte
> **Answer:** At work, a connector platform is often the right call for dozens of sources. Here the ADR records the trade-off: fewer moving parts and full visibility, at the cost of writing (and testing) the connector yourself.

### Q5. What does an `error` severity on a contract check mean?
- [ ] The pipeline crashes
- [ ] The check is skipped
- [x] The build is not published: the dashboard keeps the last good data and an incident report is written
- [ ] The failing rows are deleted
> **Answer:** `warn` checks are published and reported; `error` checks block the publish gate. Deleting rows to make a check pass would hide the problem.

### Q6. Why must every model filter lake partitions with `dt <= run_date`?
- [ ] To make queries faster
- [x] So a build for a past day (a backfill or a re-run) sees only what had arrived by then and gives the same numbers as the original run
- [ ] Because future partitions are corrupt
- [ ] dbt requires it
> **Answer:** Without it, rebuilding 15 June after September's data has landed would mix in later status changes and give different numbers than the dashboard showed on 16 June. Reproducibility needs a time boundary.

## 7. What you learned
- An architecture expressed as guarantees between steps, not as a tool list.
- Medallion layers with clear grain, mutability and access rules.
- Idempotent ingestion: half-open windows, retries with backoff, partition replacement, manifests, quarantine, PII at the door.
- A publish gate built on an atomic rename.
- Tool choices justified against requirements and a RAM budget, recorded as ADRs.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-3 phase-2-end
git show phase-2-end:spec/design.md | less
ls $(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/spec/adr; git show phase-2-end --stat
```

steps.title: Phase 3 · Implementation in four milestones: ingest, silver, gold, run
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
This is where most pipelines quietly go wrong: an order counted twice because it changed status, a payment event
delivered twice, a timestamp shifted by five and a half hours because the server runs in UTC, rupees summed as
floats, a re-run that appends a second copy of yesterday. You build the pipeline **test-first**, one milestone at a
time: delete a line from a `PENDING` list, watch its tests fail, implement until they pass. Every function and model
has a `TODO` with a hint that says where in `contract/transform-spec.md` to look and which trap to avoid. At the end,
one command ingests three months of BazaarBox data, builds silver and gold, and publishes a warehouse whose five
reports match the golden tables to the paisa.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Ingest an API with windows, pagination and retries, and file drops with validation, into idempotent lake partitions without PII (M1).
- Parse mixed time-zone timestamps, IST business dates and rupee text exactly, and build silver: the latest version per key, one row per event (M2).
- Build the gold dimensions, facts and the five reports with the exact contract columns (M3).
- Run the whole thing for a date or a range, publish atomically, and schedule it with an Airflow DAG (M4).
- Prove your gold tables equal `contract/golden/` on the fixture and on the full history.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 3.1 · The red-green loop
For every milestone:
1. Delete the milestone's line from the `PENDING` list in **every** conftest that has it
   (`pipewright/tests/conftest.py`, `tracks/<your track>/.../conftest.py`, `orchestration/tests/conftest.py`).
2. Run the tests: they fail with `NotImplementedError: Phase 3 Mx ...` (red).
3. Implement one function or model at a time, re-running the tests (green). Commit after each green step:
   `feat(pipewright): M1 HTTP client with backoff and Retry-After`.
4. Never edit a test to make it pass. If you believe a test is wrong, open an issue quoting the spec section.
```bash
make test-pipewright          # the shared package
make test-sql                 # or: make test-pyspark
make lint                     # ruff, sqlfluff, shellcheck: keep it green as you go
```
Find every stub of a milestone with `grep -rn "Phase 3 M1" pipewright tracks orchestration`.

### Step 3.2 · M1: ingestion (shared by both tracks)
Remove `"Phase 3 M1 - ingestion"`. Implement, in this order:
1. `pipewright/http.py`: `HttpClient.delay` (exponential backoff with jitter, capped; honour a numeric
   `Retry-After`) and `get_json` (bearer token, timeout, retry 429/5xx/connection errors up to `max_attempts`,
   **never** retry 401 or other 4xx; raise `SourceError` when retries run out).
2. `pipewright/lake.py`: `write_partition`: write every file into a temporary sibling directory, then swap it in
   with a rename, so a crash leaves either the old partition or the new one.
3. `pipewright/ingest.py`: `fetch_window` (the half-open window from `config.window(day)`, follow `next_cursor`),
   `conform` (drop `pii_drop` fields, reject rows missing a required field), `ingest_api`, `validate_file`,
   `ingest_file` (a missing drop raises `MissingDrop` → exit code 3).

Try it against the stub (`make source` in another terminal):
```bash
.venv/bin/pipewright ingest --all --date 2026-06-01
ls lake/raw/*/dt=2026-06-01/ && cat lake/_manifests/orders/2026-06-01.json
grep -c email lake/raw/customers/dt=2026-06-01/* || echo "no PII in the lake"
.venv/bin/pipewright ingest --all --date 2026-06-01 && find lake/raw -type f | wc -l    # same count: idempotent
SOURCE_FAULT_RATE=0.3 make source      # restart the stub with faults; ingestion must still succeed
```
The track suites use M1 too: their fixtures ingest the 3-day fixture through your code (`pipewright.testkit`).

### Step 3.3 · M2: silver (staging) models
Remove `"Phase 3 M2 - silver (staging) models"`. Start with parsing (`transform-spec.md` §2), then one model per
source (§3.1-§3.6). The tests compare every silver table with `contract/golden/fixture-silver/`.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt:** implement the macros in `tracks/sql/macros/parsing.sql` (`utc_timestamp`, `ist_date`, `to_paise`),
then the models in `models/staging/`. Read the lake with `read_json(... '{{ lake_glob("orders", "jsonl") }}' ...)`
and `filename=true` to get the partition `dt`; keep only `dt <= {{ run_date() }}`. The latest version per key is a
window function:
```sql
qualify row_number() over (partition by order_id order by updated_at_utc desc, dt desc) = 1
```
Unnest order items together with their position (`unnest(generate_series(1, len(items)))` next to `unnest(items)`
in the same select) so `line_number` is the 1-based position in the *original* array, then drop `qty <= 0`. Run one model at a time:
```bash
cd tracks/sql && ../../.venv/bin/dbt build --profiles-dir . --select stg_orders --vars '{run_date: "2026-06-03"}'
```
(The tests run dbt for you against a temporary build of the fixture; this command is for exploring.)
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark:** implement `pipewright_spark/parsing.py` (`utc_timestamp`, `ist_date`, `to_paise`,
`clean_key` as **column expressions**: no Python UDFs, so Spark can optimise them), then `staging.py`. Bronze is read
by `bronze.py` with explicit schemas. The latest version per key is a window:
```python
w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.col("updated_at_utc").desc(), F.col("dt").desc())
df.withColumn("_rn", F.row_number().over(w)).where("_rn = 1").drop("_rn")
```
Explode items with `F.posexplode` (position + 1 = `line_number`), then drop `qty <= 0`. Never let Spark parse the
offset with the session time zone: take the first 19 characters as local time and subtract the offset yourself.
```bash
make test-pyspark            # or: cd tracks/pyspark && PYTHONPATH=. ../../.venv/bin/pytest tests/test_parsing.py -x
```
<!-- /track -->

### Step 3.4 · M3: gold, the five reports
Remove `"Phase 3 M3 - gold models (the five reports)"`. Implement §4 (dims and facts) first, then §5 (the reports).
The tests compare every gold table with `contract/golden/fixture/`. The traps, report by report:
- `mart_revenue_daily`: revenue only for orders whose **latest** status is placed/shipped/delivered; `orders` is a
  *distinct* count (an order has several lines).
- `mart_cac_monthly`: new customers by the month of their first *valid* order; integer division rounded down; NULL
  CAC with no new customer; channels without spend appear with 0.
- `mart_mrr_monthly`: annual plans count `amount // 12`; a month is measured at its last day (or the run date).
- `mart_top_products_30d`: `run_date - 29 … run_date` is 30 days; ties by the lower SKU.
- `mart_cohort_retention`: only mature customers count; `retention_rate` is the only double in gold.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt:** the gold models have **enforced contracts** (`models/gold/_gold.yml`): dbt refuses to build a model
whose columns or types differ from `data-contract.yaml`, so cast explicitly (`::bigint`, `::date`). Use `{{ ref() }}`
for every upstream model so dbt builds them in order.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark:** implement the functions in `gold.py` and `pipeline.enforce()`, which selects the contract's
columns in order and casts them to the contract's types (failing loudly on a missing column). Use integer
arithmetic for money (`F.floor(a / b)` returns a double: prefer `(a - a % b) / b` cast to `long`, or `F.expr("a div b")`).
<!-- /track -->

### Step 3.5 · M4: runner, publishing and the DAG
Remove `"Phase 3 M4 - runner and orchestration"`. Implement `warehouse.publish` (refuse unless the build's
`ops.build_info.publishable` is true, then `os.replace` the build onto the published file), `runner.build_and_publish`
(transform → dq → publish, or write an incident report and raise) and `runner.run_range` (ingest every day, then
build once as of the last day). Until Phase 4, `dq.run_check` is a stub that lets every check pass.

Then fill in the DAG skeleton `orchestration/dags/pipewright_daily.py` (every `TODO(M4)`): 06:00 IST as a UTC cron,
the business date = the IST day before, `max_active_runs=1`, `check_drops` retried every 15 minutes for 3 hours, one
`ingest_<source>` task per source, then `transform` → `dq` (no retries) → `publish`. Test it with
`make setup-airflow && make test-orchestration`.

### Step 3.6 · The full run and parity
```bash
make source                               # terminal 1
make run TRACK=sql                        # terminal 2 (or TRACK=pyspark): every day, 2026-06-01 .. 2026-08-31
.venv/bin/python scripts/parity.py compare warehouse/pipewright.duckdb contract/golden/v1.0
make parity                               # both tracks on a fresh copy of the source, against golden and each other
```
`PARITY OK` means every gold table equals the reference. If one table differs, `parity.py` shows what: go back to
the spec section of that table, write a failing test on a tiny input, fix, repeat.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Implement one function from its TODO and the spec
```text
Here is a function stub with its TODO hint: <paste the stub>. Here is the rule it implements, from the spec:
<paste the transform-spec.md section>. Here is the failing test: <paste the test>. Write the implementation using
only <the standard library | DuckDB SQL in a dbt model | PySpark column expressions, no UDFs>. Explain each line
that handles an edge case (time zones, duplicates, nulls, empty input).
```
**Verify the output by:** running the milestone's tests (never only the one you pasted), reading every line you did
not write yourself, and checking the edge cases against the spec, not against the test: tests show examples, the
spec defines the rule. Note in `AI_LOG.md` what you changed.

### Prompt 2: Explain a parity difference
```text
My <SQL | PySpark> gold table <name> differs from the golden file. parity.py says: <paste the DIFF lines>. Here is
my model: <paste it>. Here is the spec section: <paste>. List the three most likely causes, and for each a 5-row
input that would prove or disprove it. Do not rewrite the model yet.
```
**Verify the output by:** building each suggested 5-row input (as a unit test or a small DuckDB query), confirming the
cause before changing code, and checking that the fix keeps every other table at `MATCH`.

### Prompt 3: Review my ingestion for idempotency and safety
```text
Here is my ingestion code: <paste ingest.py, lake.py, http.py>. Review it for: (1) what happens if the process is
killed at each line that writes, (2) whether re-running a day can duplicate or lose records, (3) retries that could
hammer the API or retry a request that will never succeed, (4) any path by which an email or phone number could be
written or logged. Answer with line references.
```
**Verify the output by:** turning each real finding into a test (kill = raise an exception in a fake writer; re-run =
call twice and compare the lake), and rejecting "findings" you cannot reproduce. Never paste real tokens or rows.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] All four Phase 3 groups removed from every `PENDING` list; `make test-pipewright`, `make test-<track>` and `make test-orchestration` green.
- [ ] `make lint` green.
- [ ] `make run TRACK=<your track>` publishes `warehouse/pipewright.duckdb` for 2026-08-31.
- [ ] `parity.py compare` against `contract/golden/v1.0` prints `PARITY OK` (and `make parity` if you have Java).
- [ ] Small commits per green step, with Conventional Commit messages.
- [ ] `AI_LOG.md` entries for this phase, including one AI-written piece of code you had to fix.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. An order appears in the lake on 1 June (placed) and on 4 June (cancelled). What does silver keep?
- [ ] Both rows, so the history is visible
- [x] One row: the latest version by `updated_at` (then `dt`), with status `cancelled`
- [ ] The first row, because it has the original amount
- [ ] Neither: changed orders are suspicious
> **Answer:** Bronze keeps both deliveries (immutable history); silver keeps the latest state per `order_id` (§3.1). Keeping both would double-count the order's lines in revenue.

### Q2. Why must `HttpClient` never retry a 401?
- [ ] 401 responses are slow
- [x] A wrong or missing token will not fix itself; retrying wastes time and can lock the account, so it must fail fast with a clear error
- [ ] The API forbids retries
- [ ] Retries are only for GET requests
> **Answer:** Retry what is transient (429, 5xx, timeouts), fail fast on what is not (401, 404, 400). Honour `Retry-After` when the server tells you how long to wait.

### Q3. `2026-06-01T19:00:00Z`: which business date is it?
- [ ] 2026-06-01
- [x] 2026-06-02 (19:00 UTC + 5:30 = 00:30 IST the next day)
- [ ] It depends on the server
- [ ] 2026-05-31
> **Answer:** `ist_date(ts) = date(ts + 5h30)`. Grouping by the UTC date puts every order between 00:00 and 05:30 IST on the wrong day; the fixture contains such orders on purpose.

### Q4. Why does `line_number` keep the position in the *original* items array even when a line with `qty <= 0` is dropped?
- [ ] To save a column
- [x] So the key `(order_id, line_number)` of every kept line is stable: dropping or fixing another line never renumbers it
- [ ] Because dbt requires sequential numbers
- [ ] It does not matter
> **Answer:** Keys that shift when unrelated data changes break incremental updates, joins with downstream systems and parity between tracks.

### Q5. Why is the warehouse published with `os.replace` instead of writing the tables directly into it?
- [ ] It is faster
- [ ] DuckDB cannot overwrite tables
- [x] The rename is atomic: the dashboard sees the complete old build or the complete new build, never a half-written one
- [ ] To keep a backup automatically
> **Answer:** Write to a build file, check it, then swap. A crash or a failed check before the swap leaves the published file untouched.

### Q6. Your PySpark CAC uses `F.floor(spend / customers)` and one row differs from golden by 1 paisa. Why?
- [ ] Spark has a bug
- [x] `/` produces a double; for large values a double cannot represent every integer quotient exactly, so flooring it can be off by one; integer division avoids it
- [ ] The golden file is wrong
- [ ] Customers should be a double
> **Answer:** Money stays integer end to end. Use integer division (`div`) so both tracks round down exactly as the spec says.

## 7. What you learned
- Test-first implementation with a pending list: red, green, commit.
- Ingestion that survives retries, crashes and re-runs, and keeps PII out.
- Exact parsing: offsets by hand, IST business dates, rupee text to integer paise.
- Silver as "latest version per key" and "one row per event", with window functions in SQL or Spark.
- Gold tables with enforced contracts, five reports with their traps, and an atomic publish.
- Parity against golden tables as the definition of "done".

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-4 phase-3-end
git diff phase-2-end phase-3-end --stat
git diff phase-2-end phase-3-end -- tracks/sql        # or tracks/pyspark, pipewright
```

steps.title: Phase 4 · Data tests and data-quality checks: the publish gate
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Unit tests prove your code does what you meant on the inputs you thought of. Data does not care what you thought
of: tomorrow the source sends a status nobody announced, a catalogue drop forgets a SKU, a join fans out after a
schema change. A pipeline needs a second kind of test that runs **on every build, on the real data, before anyone
sees it**: data tests and data-quality checks. In this phase you switch on the checks declared in the data contract,
write the dbt data tests and unit tests (SQL track), add a coverage gate, and see the publish gate do its job: a
build that fails a blocking check is never published, and an incident report explains why.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Explain the difference between unit tests (code, small inputs), data tests (properties of the real tables) and data-quality checks (the gate before publishing).
- Implement the contract's check kinds: `row_count_min/max`, `accepted_values`, `relationship`, `max_share`, `expression`, `reconcile`, with severities.
- Record only aggregates in the report (never a row), and mask unexpected values that might be personal data.
- Write dbt generic, singular and unit tests (SQL track) or rely on the shared checks plus a coverage gate (PySpark track).
- Break the data on purpose and watch the gate keep the last good build.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 4.1 · Three kinds of tests
Write one sentence each in your notes, then read on:
- **Unit test:** a function or model on a tiny, hand-made input (`test_parsing.py`, a dbt unit test). Runs in CI.
- **Data test:** a property every row or table must have (`order_id` is unique, every order's customer exists, revenue
  reconciles to the lines). Runs on every build, on the real data.
- **Data-quality check with a severity:** a data test wired to a decision: `error` blocks publishing, `warn` is
  published and reported. Lives in `contract/data-contract.yaml` so both tracks share it.

### Step 4.2 · Implement the contract's checks (shared)
Remove `"Phase 4 - data-quality checks"` from every `PENDING` list. Implement `pipewright/dq.py`'s `run_check`: one
branch per kind. Each runs **one aggregate query** against the build and returns a `CheckResult` with `observed`,
`threshold` and `status`:
- `accepted_values`: count rows outside the list (`@order_status` resolves to the contract's enum); report up to 5
  distinct unexpected values, masked unless they match `SAFE_VALUE` (a code is fine, an email is not).
- `relationship`: count child keys with no parent. `max_share`: the share of rows matching `where`.
- `reconcile`: two queries that must return the same number (revenue = revenue lines).
- A check that cannot run (bad SQL, unknown kind) is status `error`, **never** a pass.
```bash
make test-pipewright
.venv/bin/pipewright dq --date 2026-08-31 && cat warehouse/reports/dq-2026-08-31.json | head -40
```

### Step 4.3 · Data tests in your track
Remove `"Phase 4 - data tests"`.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt:** add tests until `test_dbt_tests.py` passes (at least 60 data tests and 3 unit tests, all green):
1. **Generic tests in YAML** (`models/staging/_staging.yml`, `models/gold/_gold.yml`): `unique`, `not_null`,
   `accepted_values`, `relationships` on every key and enum column (dbt 1.12 syntax:
   `data_tests: [{accepted_values: {arguments: {values: [...]}}}]`).
2. **Your own generic tests** in `tests/generic/`: `non_negative`, `positive`, `accepted_range`,
   `unique_combination` (a test is a query that returns the failing rows):
   ```sql
   {% test non_negative(model, column_name) %}
   select {{ column_name }} from {{ model }} where {{ column_name }} < 0
   {% endtest %}
   ```
3. **Singular tests** in `tests/singular/`: no order after the run date, gross = lines, revenue reconciles, cohorts
   add up, the parsing macros on known inputs.
4. **Unit tests** (`models/gold/_unit_tests.yml`): mock inputs → expected rows for the trickiest rules (CAC rounding
   and NULL, mature-only retention, annual MRR as 1/12).
```bash
cd tracks/sql && ../../.venv/bin/dbt test --profiles-dir . --select test_type:unit      # after a build
make test-sql
```
On this track `pipewright dq` also runs `dbt test` (data tests only) and merges the results into the same report,
so a failing dbt test blocks publishing like a contract check.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark:** your data tests are the **shared contract checks**: they run on the warehouse whatever track
built it, so they test your Spark output exactly as they test the dbt output. Run them on a full build:
```bash
make run TRACK=pyspark && .venv/bin/pipewright dq --date 2026-08-31
```
Then turn on the **coverage gate** (Step 4.4) and add edge-case unit tests with tiny DataFrames for anything the
fixture does not cover well (an order exactly at 00:00 IST, a payment delivered twice on two days, an unknown
city). Spark tests are slow to start: share one `SparkSession` per test session (the `spark` fixture) and build
DataFrames with explicit schemas.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 4.4 · A coverage gate
Add `fail_under = 85` to `[tool.coverage.report]` in `pipewright/pyproject.toml` (and `tracks/pyspark/pyproject.toml`
on the PySpark track). `make test-pipewright` now fails if less than 85 % of the lines ran. Look at the report's
missing lines: an untested branch in ingestion or in a check is exactly where a 3 a.m. surprise hides. Coverage is a
floor, not a goal: 100 % covered code can still compute the wrong revenue; that is what the golden tables are for.

### Step 4.5 · Break it on purpose: the gate in action
Prove the gate works, end to end, on a copy of the data:
```bash
cp -r source-data /tmp/broken && sed -i 's/"status":"delivered"/"status":"lost"/' /tmp/broken/api/orders.jsonl
# restart the stub on /tmp/broken (python -m bazaarbox_source serve --data /tmp/broken --port 18140), then:
.venv/bin/pipewright run --date 2026-08-31; echo "exit $?"
ls warehouse/reports/ && .venv/bin/pipewright explain           # the incident note (template until Phase 6)
```
Expected: `status_accepted` fails with `observed` > 0 and the value `lost`, exit 1, nothing published, the dashboard's
warehouse still at the last good date. Restore the real source afterwards. Write down what you saw: Phase 7 opens
with the day this happens for real.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Propose data tests from a schema
```text
Here is the schema and description of a gold table: <paste one model from _gold.yml or data-contract.yaml>, and the
rule that builds it: <paste the transform-spec.md section>. Propose data tests: which columns need unique / not_null /
accepted_values / relationships, which cross-table reconciliations prove nothing is lost or duplicated, and which
edge cases deserve a unit test with mock rows. Mark each as error or warn and justify the severity.
```
**Verify the output by:** running each proposed test on the fixture build and on the full build (a test that fails on
correct data is wrong, not strict), checking every `accepted_values` list against the contract's enums, and
discussing any severity you disagree with in your PR.

### Prompt 2: Write a dbt unit test or a PySpark edge-case test
```text
Rule: <paste one rule, e.g. CAC = spend // new customers, NULL with no new customer>. Write a <dbt unit test in YAML
(given: mock rows for each input model, expect: rows) | pytest test building tiny PySpark DataFrames with explicit
schemas> that covers: the normal case, the boundary, and the empty or NULL case. Use at most 5 input rows.
```
**Verify the output by:** computing the expected rows by hand before running the test, making the test fail once on
purpose (change the rule) to prove it can fail, and checking the mock rows' columns match the real model's.

### Prompt 3: Make a check report safe to share
```text
Here is a data-quality report my pipeline writes: <paste a dq-*.json with fake values>. It will be read by on-call
engineers and sent to an AI model for an incident summary. List every field that could carry personal or secret
data, and how to keep the report useful with aggregates only.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking each suggestion against `dq.py` (what is really written), testing the masking with
a value that looks like an email, and keeping the report useful: an incident note must still say *which* check failed
and *how much*.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] Both Phase 4 groups removed from every `PENDING` list; all suites green.
- [ ] `run_check` implements every check kind; a check that cannot run is an error.
- [ ] SQL track: ≥ 60 dbt data tests and ≥ 3 unit tests passing; PySpark track: edge-case tests added.
- [ ] Coverage gate at 85 % in the shared package (and the PySpark track).
- [ ] The break-it experiment: a screenshot or log of the blocked publish and the incident note, in your PR.
- [ ] `AI_LOG.md` entries, including a test the AI proposed that was wrong.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. What is the difference between a unit test and a data test?
- [ ] There is none
- [x] A unit test checks code on small hand-made inputs in CI; a data test checks a property of the real tables on every build
- [ ] Data tests are slower unit tests
- [ ] Unit tests are only for Python
> **Answer:** Code can be correct and the data still wrong (a new status, a missing SKU). You need both: unit tests before merging, data tests before publishing.

### Q2. A check fails because 41 orders have a status the contract does not know. What should happen?
- [ ] Map the new status to `placed` and continue
- [ ] Delete the 41 orders
- [x] Block the publish (severity error), keep the last good warehouse, write an incident report naming the unexpected value
- [ ] Publish with a warning
> **Answer:** An unknown status could be revenue or a loss; guessing silently changes the CEO's numbers. The contract decides, and changing it is a versioned decision (Phase 7).

### Q3. Why must a check that cannot run (e.g. a SQL error) be reported as `error`, not `pass`?
- [ ] To make the report longer
- [x] A check that silently passes when it is broken gives false confidence: the gate would be open exactly when it is blind
- [ ] Because DuckDB raises exceptions
- [ ] It should be skipped instead
> **Answer:** Fail closed. A broken smoke detector must beep, not stay quiet.

### Q4. Why does the report store "41 rows, values: lost" and never the 41 rows themselves?
- [ ] Rows are too big
- [x] The report is shared with on-call engineers and an AI model: aggregates and safe codes are enough to act on, rows could contain personal data
- [ ] JSON cannot store rows
- [ ] dbt does not return rows
> **Answer:** Design reports so they can be shared. Values that do not look like a code are masked for the same reason.

### Q5. What does `reconcile` between `mart_revenue_daily` and `fct_order_items` catch?
- [ ] Slow queries
- [x] A join or filter that drops or duplicates revenue between the facts and the report, even when every column looks valid
- [ ] Wrong column types
- [ ] Missing indexes
> **Answer:** Column tests cannot see a fan-out: every row is valid, there are just too many. Totals that must agree across layers can.

### Q6. Your coverage is 92 %. Does that mean the revenue is right?
- [ ] Yes, above 85 % is correct
- [x] No: coverage says which lines ran, not whether they compute the right number; the golden tables and reconciliation checks test correctness
- [ ] Only if it is 100 %
- [ ] Coverage does not apply to data pipelines
> **Answer:** Coverage finds untested code; it cannot find a wrong rule that is tested with a wrong expectation.

## 7. What you learned
- Unit tests, data tests and data-quality checks, and where each runs.
- Declarative checks in a shared contract, with severities that drive a publish decision.
- dbt generic, custom generic, singular and unit tests; or shared checks plus edge-case tests for Spark.
- Reports with aggregates only, masking anything that is not a safe code.
- A coverage gate as a floor, and a deliberate failure to prove the gate works.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-5 phase-4-end
git diff phase-3-end phase-4-end --stat
git diff phase-3-end phase-4-end -- tracks/sql/tests tracks/sql/models
```

steps.title: Phase 5 · CI: dbt build and tests on the fixture, cross-track parity
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
A pipeline's code changes far more often than its sources: a "harmless" refactor of a join, a dbt upgrade, a new
column. Each can move a number the CEO reads tomorrow. Continuous integration runs every check on every pull
request, on a clean machine, before the change is merged: lint, the unit tests, **`dbt build` with all its tests on
the committed fixture**, the DAG tests, and the strongest check of all: both tracks run the full history and must
produce the golden tables and each other's tables, row by row. In this phase you replace the starter's simple CI
with that pipeline, learn every GitHub Actions concept it uses, and make one check, `ci-ok`, the gate for merging.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Read and write a GitHub Actions workflow: triggers, jobs, `needs`, `if`, matrix, caching, outputs, artifacts, permissions.
- Run each part only when its files changed (path filters) without blocking pull requests (an aggregator job).
- Check in CI that the committed fixture and manifest are exactly what the seeded generator produces.
- Run `dbt build` (models, data tests, unit tests, contracts) on the fixture, and the PySpark suite with Java, in CI.
- Run the full-history parity of both tracks in CI and publish its result on the run page.
- Keep CI's tool versions identical to your laptop's, and protect `main` with required checks.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 5.1 · Read the starter CI and the explainer
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the starter: one matrix job per part, `make install/lint/test-<part>`) next to
`docs/github-actions-explained.md` §1-§6. Answer for yourself: which event starts it, how many jobs run, where the
Python version comes from, why `fail-fast: false`.

### Step 5.2 · Design the full pipeline
Sketch the jobs and their dependencies before writing YAML:
```text
changes ─┬─ contract        (fixture + manifest reproducible, shellcheck, CMS export)
         ├─ pipewright      (lint + tests + coverage gate)
         ├─ sql ──────┐     (sqlfluff + dbt build on the fixture + expected tables)
         ├─ pyspark ──┼─ parity   (full history, both tracks = golden, sql = pyspark)
         ├─ orchestration   (DAG tests, Airflow constraints)
         └──────────────┴─ ci-ok   (fails if anything failed; skipped is fine)
```
Keep the job names `pipewright · lint + unit`, `sql · lint + unit`, `pyspark · lint + unit`: branch protection
already requires them.

### Step 5.3 · Write the workflow
Replace `.github/workflows/ci.yml` step by step (the reference is `git show phase-5-end:.github/workflows/ci.yml`;
write yours first):
1. `changes` with `dorny/paths-filter@v3` and an `all` output that is true on pushes or when shared files changed
   (`github-actions-explained.md` §7).
2. `contract`: regenerate the 3-day fixture into `$RUNNER_TEMP` and `diff -r` it with `contract/fixture/source`;
   regenerate the full source with `--check contract/source-manifest-*.json`; `shellcheck scripts/*.sh`;
   `python3 scripts/build-cms.py --check`.
3. One job per part with `actions/setup-python@v5` (Python 3.12, `cache: pip`), `actions/setup-java@v4` (Temurin 21)
   for PySpark, and the same `make` targets you run locally.
4. `orchestration`: install Airflow **with its constraints file** and run `make test-orchestration`.
5. `parity`: both tracks + Java, then `scripts/parity-run.sh <version>`; append the output to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`.
6. `ci-ok`: `if: always()`, `needs:` everything, fail on `failure` or `cancelled`.

Lint it before pushing: `actionlint` (<https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint>) catches typos in expressions and
runs shellcheck on every `run:` block.

<!-- track:sql -->
**SQL · dbt track:** the `sql` job is where dbt runs in CI: `make test-sql` builds the fixture with `dbt build` (seeds,
models, contracts, data tests, unit tests) through the same runner as production, then compares silver and gold with
the expected files. Add `--warn-error-options` only if you want warnings to fail too (we allow `warn` severity). The
`target/` folder is never committed: CI starts clean, so a model that only works because of a stale artifact fails here.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:pyspark -->
**Python · PySpark track:** the `pyspark` job needs `actions/setup-java@v4` before the tests, or Spark fails with
"JAVA_HOME is not set". Spark is slow to start: one session per test run (the `spark` fixture), `local[2]`, and a
`timeout-minutes` on the job so a hung JVM cannot burn six hours of free minutes.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 5.4 · Dependabot
Add `.github/dependabot.yml` with weekly updates for `github-actions` and `pip` (`/pipewright`, `/tracks/sql`,
`/tracks/pyspark`). Every Dependabot PR runs the full CI, so an upgrade that moves a number is caught by parity.
Airflow is bumped by hand together with its constraints URL.

### Step 5.5 · Push, watch, protect
1. Push a branch and open a PR: watch the jobs start, the skipped ones, and `ci-ok`.
2. Make it fail on purpose: change one rule (e.g. `>= 0` to `> 0` in a model), push, and read the `parity` summary.
   Revert.
3. In **your fork**: Settings → Branches → add a rule for `main`: require a pull request, require status checks
   (`ci-ok`, or the three `· lint + unit` checks), require branches to be up to date, no force pushes.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Explain a workflow line by line
```text
Here is a GitHub Actions workflow: <paste ci.yml>. Explain it to a data engineer who has never used Actions: what
triggers it, which jobs run in which order and why, what each `if:` decides, what is cached and with which key.
Then list three ways it could silently stop checking something (e.g. a job that is always skipped).
```
**Verify the output by:** checking each claim against `docs/github-actions-explained.md` and the official docs, and
testing the "silently stops checking" scenarios with a PR that touches only `docs/` and one that touches
`tracks/sql/`.

### Prompt 2: Debug a red CI job
```text
This CI job fails but the same command passes on my laptop. Job log (last 60 lines): <paste>. Workflow job: <paste
the job>. My local versions: <python --version, java -version, pip freeze | grep -E "dbt|pyspark|duckdb">. What
differs between the two environments, and which single command reproduces CI locally?
```
**Verify the output by:** reproducing the failure locally with a clean checkout (`git clone` into a temp folder, then
the job's commands) before changing anything, and keeping versions pinned in both places, never "latest".

### Prompt 3: Review my CI for security and cost
```text
Review this workflow for least privilege, secret exposure, supply-chain risk and wasted minutes: <paste ci.yml>.
For each finding: the line, the risk, the fix. Do not suggest paid services.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking `permissions:` is `contents: read` by default, that no secret is needed at all,
that every job has `timeout-minutes`, and running `actionlint` after the changes.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] A full `.github/workflows/ci.yml`: changes, contract, pipewright, sql, pyspark, orchestration, parity, ci-ok.
- [ ] `actionlint` passes with no findings.
- [ ] A green run on `main` with the parity summary on the run page.
- [ ] A PR that failed parity on purpose (link it), then was fixed.
- [ ] `.github/dependabot.yml`.
- [ ] Branch protection on your fork's `main`.
- [ ] `AI_LOG.md` entry.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why not use `on: push: paths:` to skip CI when only docs change?
- [ ] It is not supported for pull requests
- [x] A skipped workflow never reports its checks, so a required check stays "pending" and blocks the PR forever; per-job `if:` with an aggregator job avoids it
- [ ] It is slower
- [ ] Paths only work with tags
> **Answer:** Always run the workflow, decide per job, and require `ci-ok`, which treats skipped jobs as fine.

### Q2. What does the `contract` job's `diff -r` of a regenerated fixture prove?
- [ ] The fixture is small
- [x] The committed fixture is exactly what the seeded generator produces, so nobody hand-edited it to make a test pass
- [ ] The generator is fast
- [ ] The API stub works
> **Answer:** Test data is code. If it can drift from its generator, a failing test can be "fixed" by editing the data.

### Q3. Why does CI install Airflow with a constraints file?
- [ ] It is faster
- [x] Airflow has hundreds of transitive dependencies; the constraints pin all of them to versions tested together, the same as locally and in the Docker image
- [ ] Airflow refuses to install otherwise
- [ ] To install the Postgres provider
> **Answer:** Without pins, a new release of some dependency can break the DAG tests overnight with no change on your side.

### Q4. The `parity` job runs the full history through both tracks. Why is the fixture not enough?
- [ ] The fixture has no orders
- [x] Three days cannot exercise month boundaries, 30-day windows, cohort maturity or late status changes across weeks; the full history can, and the two tracks must agree on all of it
- [ ] dbt needs at least 30 days
- [ ] The golden files only cover the full history
> **Answer:** The fixture is for fast, hand-checkable unit tests; parity on three months is the end-to-end proof.

### Q5. CI is red, your laptop is green. What is the first thing to compare?
- [ ] The color of the terminal
- [x] Tool versions (Python, Java, dbt, PySpark, DuckDB) and untracked files on your laptop (a `target/`, a `lake/`, a local seed)
- [ ] The GitHub status page
- [ ] The number of CPU cores
> **Answer:** CI starts from a clean checkout with pinned versions. Most "works on my machine" bugs are a version or a file that exists only on your machine.

### Q6. Which permission does Pipewright's CI need?
- [ ] `contents: write` to commit results
- [ ] `packages: write`
- [x] `contents: read` (and `pull-requests: read` for the path filter); nothing else, no secrets
- [ ] An admin token
> **Answer:** Least privilege: CI reads code and reports checks. The pipeline's production runs are Airflow's job, not CI's.

## 7. What you learned
- GitHub Actions: triggers, jobs, `needs`, `if`, matrix, caching, outputs, step summaries, permissions.
- Path filters with an aggregator job, and why required checks must always report.
- dbt build and tests on a fixture in CI; Spark with Java in CI; Airflow with constraints.
- Reproducible test data checked in CI, and full-history parity of two implementations as the merge gate.
- Dependabot and actionlint; branch protection with required checks.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-6 phase-5-end
git diff phase-4-end phase-5-end -- .github
```

steps.title: Phase 6 · v1.0: the scheduled pipeline, the dashboard, the AI explainer, Docker
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Until now the pipeline runs when you type a command. A data product runs **every morning without you**: Airflow
starts it at 06:00 IST, waits for late files, retries what is flaky, never retries a failed check, and the CEO opens a
dashboard that says which day it shows. When a check blocks the publish, the on-call engineer gets an incident note
that says what failed and what to try first. In this phase you build the Streamlit dashboard, the optional AI incident
explainer with guardrails and an offline fallback, the Docker images and Compose stack (non-root, read-only, under
6 GB), an acceptance check that runs all of it in CI, a runbook, and you release **v1.0.0**.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Build a dashboard that reads only the published warehouse, shows its business date and the five reports, and is tested in CI.
- Add an AI feature safely: only aggregate facts go out, the answer is checked by guardrails, and every failure falls back to a deterministic template.
- Package every component in small, non-root Docker images with read-only file systems, and wire them with Compose profiles.
- Run the Airflow DAG end to end in a container, on Postgres, and read its logs.
- Prove the release with one acceptance script (images, pipelines in containers, parity, smoke tests, AI provider down, no secrets in logs).
- Write a runbook and release v1.0.0 with a CHANGELOG.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 6.1 · The dashboard
Remove `"Phase 6 - dashboard"` from the `PENDING` lists. The dashboard (`dashboard/app.py` + `dashboard/data.py`) has
one tab per report plus a *Data health* tab. Rules:
- read `warehouse/pipewright.duckdb` **read-only**, never the build file;
- show "Data as of <business date>" and the age in days at the top; a stale dashboard must say so;
- format money from paise as ₹ with Indian digit grouping (₹3,98,25,047), computed in Python, not in SQL strings;
- keep queries in `data.py` (testable without Streamlit); `app.py` only lays out.
```bash
make install-dashboard && make test-dashboard
make dashboard                       # http://127.0.0.1:18142 on the warehouse from your last `make run`
```
The tests use Streamlit's `AppTest` to render every tab against a small warehouse built from the fixture.

### Step 6.2 · The AI incident explainer (optional at runtime, required in tests)
Remove `"Phase 6 - AI incident explainer"`. Implement `pipewright/explainer.py`'s `validate` and `explain`:
1. **Facts, not data:** `facts_from(report)` turns the failed checks into numbered facts (`[1] status_accepted
   failed: 41 rows outside the enum, values: lost`). Only these facts are sent: no rows, no customer ids.
2. **Provider:** `AI_PROVIDER=template` (default) never calls anything. `AI_PROVIDER=openai` calls any
   OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`AI_BASE_URL`, `AI_MODEL`, optional `AI_API_KEY`): Ollama locally
   (`http://localhost:11434/v1`), or a free tier. No paid key is ever required.
